The rules depart from ordinary dodgeball: a hit does not send an infield player out but drains health, and a team loses once its three infielders are eliminated. Each player has individual stats and special power shots, called magic balls, thrown from a run-up or a running jump. Because of sprite limits all players are drawn at the same size. Opponents include Hanazono High School and national teams such as England, India, Iceland and China. A two-player versus mode was added, and the club practice mode allows four-player matches with a multitap.

t_276e4606084e.overview: Tied to the Photon toy license, Takara's maze game sends a soldier through a multi-floor dungeon shown in pseudo-3D from behind the character. Rather than a role-playing game, it plays as a shooter: the player explores, shoots down alien creatures as they pass, and collects items. Turning left or right rotates the view by 90 degrees, and since much of the maze looks identical, a compass and a coordinate counter help with navigation. Twelve disks each hold a hint, but a loader must be found before any can be read. Cards open certain doors, a sensor makes secret walls easier to find, colored stones allow safe passage down matching vertical shafts, and a teleporter jumps back to a placed marker. Hit points start with a maximum of 1000 and can be raised as high as 9999.

t_2779772d1ad9.overview: Based on the Taiwanese Xiao Ma Li gambling machines and carrying the English title Big TV Mary Bar, the game challenges the player to gain as many credits as possible by betting on the icons of a slot-machine board. Two controllers are required: each button on the first, including the D-pad, places a bet on a certain icon, while the Bar icon is bet with A on the second controller and B starts the machine. After a win, pressing up starts a bonus card game in which guessing whether the next card is high or low doubles the winnings. When the pointer lands on the coin, "Push Start To Rich" flashes and tapping Start makes a Mario lookalike jump into a block for 10 credits each time.

t_281734e6c7df.overview: A prince must make his way through Groken Castle to rescue Princess Margarita in this puzzle-action sequel to The Castle. Progress depends on pushing objects: in some rooms, brick blocks, barrels, candles and elevator controlling blocks must be lined up before the next room can be reached. A door opens only with a key of matching color, and only while the prince stands beside it, not in mid-jump. A map found in the first room shows a grid of 10x10 rooms and marks where the princess is held. Knights, bishops, wizards, fire spirits, vikings and phantom flowers must be avoided, though the prince can also strike with his sword at very close range. Rooms are wider than the screen and scroll sideways, play starts with four lives, and progress can be saved to the Famicom Data Recorder or ASCII Turbo File.

t_2818d8dab051.overview:
Controlling the mouse Mappy, the player gathers gifts scattered across themed environments while evading antagonistic cats. Progression requires navigating through eight areas, such as Railroad Town and Ghost Town, using ladders and trampolines to move between floors. Each stage requires finding the required target items—such as cheese, wedding rings, Christmas trees, or baseballs—before reaching the right-hand exit. If an exit is closed, a hidden entrance must be found to explore a sub-area for a necessary item to proceed.

Defense relies on portable protection weapons like toys, gold coins, pots, and fish to divert or incapacitate pursuers. Stages also contain fighting weapons such as bowling balls and flashlights to defeat enemies temporarily. The game spans four stories, culminating in Muky Town before delivering the collected presents to the castle.

t_283af81167c0.overview: Loosely adapted from the 16th-century Chinese epic novel of the same name, this role-playing game unfolds during the final days of the Shang dynasty. Nezha, son of the general Li Jing, sets out to defeat the tyrant King Zhou, and the story follows a group of ordinary humans who unite against his rule rather than the gods and spirits of the novel. Ne Zha wields three powerful artifacts granted by the god Tai Yi. Most of the adventure is spent fighting random enemies to gain experience points and level up. Battles are turn-based and viewed mostly from a first-person perspective, with actions selected from a menu in Dragon Quest style; characters can use physical attacks or cast magic.

t_284c96fca0f3.overview: This historical strategy game has the player govern the provinces of China with the aim of unifying the entire land. All five scenarios of the computer original are included, starting between 189 and 215 across a map of 58 provinces; early scenarios are won by controlling 30 or 40 provinces, the last only by taking all 58. Up to eight players can compete. Rulers recruit officers by visiting in person or sending fine horses or beauties, and diplomacy works through gifts and marriage rather than alliances. In war, each unit is led by one general, with up to ten units per side, and attackers win by occupying every castle hex or defeating the defending ruler. On the Famicom, plunder and wandering commands are absent, battles have no charge or tactic commands, and an attack unresolved within 30 days counts as a loss.

t_2869e2c4dd84.overview: Super-deformed Ultraman Club heroes and monsters meet for a track-and-field sports day, played with a barcode-reader add-on. Scanned barcodes become athletes rated for power, stamina and speed, or items, and 40 included cards allow immediate play without collecting barcodes. The main cup mode pits three four-member teams against one another over seven events: an automatically run relay road race, managed through stamina settings, alongside the 100-meter dash, long jump, shot put, 110-meter hurdles, clay shooting and triple jump, with points for each result deciding the overall winner. Up to two human players take part, and the computer fills the remaining places. A world-record challenge lets any of the six standard events be played individually, and a test mode shows a scanned barcode's data. There is no single-player stage-clearing mode.

t_286cc4d7a313.overview: Its Japanese title translates to Jumping Kid: The Tale of Jack and the Beanstalk, and the game is a variation on that famous fairy tale. Designed for a single player, it is a challenging platform game whose play is often likened to Mega Man. Bean power-ups strengthen the hero's attacks, while springs increase the height of his jumps.

t_28861814eb53.overview: Three slot machines, Cutie Bunny, Juicy Fruits and Las Vegas, are on offer in this adult slot machine simulation, each with a distinct visual design and musical score. After purchasing medallions, the player bets up to five on every pull, stops the reels one at a time with the D-pad, and can switch to another machine between spins. Each machine has its own scantily clad hostess, who appears when winnings surpass certain thresholds and loses more of her clothing as the net profit grows, finally appearing nude.

t_28f44b27957f.overview:
A martial artist named Thomas climbs the five floors of a castle to rescue Sylvia, who is held captive by a mysterious gang led by Mr. X. The player guides Thomas along side-scrolling floors, climbing the stairs to the next floor after clearing each area.

Controlling Thomas, players execute punches and kicks from standing, crouching, or jumping positions. Strikes fend off regular adversaries, such as Grippers, Knife Throwers, and Tom Toms, alongside hazards like objects dropping from the ceiling, snakes, and fire-breathing dragons. When enemies catch Thomas, his energy drains until the player breaks free with quick button presses. Each floor features a time limit and concludes with a duel against a boss, from the Stick Fighter up to Mr. X himself. Rescuing Sylvia on the top floor leads to the next round. Game A suits beginners and Game B experts, and a two-player option is included.

t_2924c90a3094.overview: Kantaro, a fireworks craftsman who has finished his training in Kyoto, heads home toward Edo, where Momoko, the woman he loves, is waiting. The stages of this side-scrolling action game are modeled on the 53 post towns of the old Tokaido road, ending with the leg from Shinagawa to Nihonbashi. Kantaro's firecracker balls fly in an arc with limited range, so some enemies cannot be hit with a normal throw; crouching sets one on the ground to explode after a delay. He has no life gauge, and touching an enemy or projectile or falling into a hole costs a life. Gold koban coins pay for crossing flooded rivers and passing checkpoints without a permit, and collecting ten reveals an entrance to a hidden warp route. One or two players take turns.

t_29687354cd6a.overview: Battles switch to a command system in the third strategy entry of the series, and each unit is now made up of five mobile suits. Every character carries a level that changes hit and evasion rates. Scenario maps come in four types: Earth, space, Sengoku and Gaiden. A side wins by wiping out the opposing force or by occupying the enemy Gachapolis, which becomes the main keep in the Sengoku maps, whichever comes first. The Knight Gundam scenario is won by defeating Satan Gundam, who is fixed at the top level of 20 with very high hit and evasion rates, so fighting him without leveling up is nearly hopeless. Player 1 can also use AEUG units and Player 2 Titans units. One or two players can take part.

t_297884662cdf.overview: Based on the biblical story of the same name, the platform game puts the player in control of Noah as he rescues different animals across the world. The journey covers seven worlds, each tied to a continent and time period, with three stages per world for 21 stages in total. During each stage the water slowly rises, making Noah harder to maneuver. Ducks give him different weapons, and other items make him invulnerable or freeze enemies. Partway through the stages Noah faces a drainplug monster, and every third stage ends with a large boss fight. Play is for a single player.

t_2990af61d516.overview: A knight named Sir Arthur sets out to rescue Princess Prin-Prin, who has been kidnapped by Astaroth, fighting zombies, demons and other monsters along the way. Arthur can pick up new weapons, bonuses and extra suits of armor, but he can withstand only two hits: the first knocks off his armor and the second costs a life. A life is also lost if a level is not completed within a set time limit. Some bosses cannot be defeated with certain weapons, such as the dragon with the lance. Defeating Astaroth is not the end, since the entire game must then be replayed on a higher difficulty level to reach the genuine final ending.

t_29ad49b85711.overview: Drawing its cast from the novel The Legend of the Condor Heroes, this Famicom fighting game, also known as Kung Fu Legend, has no relation to SNK's World Heroes series despite its English title. It runs on the same engine as Super Fighter III: A punches and B kicks, with a tap giving a light attack and holding the button a strong one, and throws are performed by holding backward or forward and pressing A near the opponent. Eight characters reinterpret figures from the novel under generic names such as Beauty Jenny, Flying Dragon, Odd Old Man, Drunken Beggar and Tyrant, each with special moves. The single-player game is a fight through all eight opponents in a fixed order, rewarded with an ending of a single image.

t_29f67c57b54b.overview: Drawn from the first story of the MADARA manga, this Konami role-playing game is set in a mythological era and follows Madara, a goodhearted teenage boy who uses fantastic prosthetic limbs called gimmicks and a legendary sword to fight his own father, the evil overlord Miroku. Because the original comic was still unfinished when the game was made, the second half of the story is original to the game, and the handling of the eight demon generals differs slightly from the comic. Unlike the Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest role-playing games of the time, combat involves movement around battlefields rather than stationary turn-by-turn exchanges. The large cartridge also uses the VRC6 sound enhancement chip found in Akumajō Densetsu.

t_2a0b262ed563.overview: A lone soldier, Super Joe, has to fight his way out singlehandedly against a massive assault of enemy troops in this shooter. He carries an assault rifle with unlimited ammunition and a limited supply of hand grenades that can only be thrown toward the top of the screen. Along the way, prisoners of war being transported across the screen by the enemy can be freed. This home version adds hidden underground shelters that can only be opened with grenades, holding more prisoners to rescue. Power-ups include a stronger machine gun and unlimited grenades, both lost when a life is lost, and special glasses reveal all the hidden bunkers. The course is built from four unique level designs.

t_2a178534089a.overview: Set in a small American town, this platformer follows a young man called Kid, who takes on pizza delivery to earn the money for a ring for his girlfriend Betty. Each job sends him to various dangerous locations, where many enemies get in the way, among them his rival Nick, who is trying to steal Betty away. The route runs across seven stages plus bonus levels. Points are scored at the end of each stage based on how quickly it was completed, with extra points for defeating enemies and recovering extra pizzas. Developed by Arc System Works and originally published by Jaleco for the Famicom, the game was later issued on an NES cartridge by Broke Studio with a full English translation, improved hitbox detection and PAL/NTSC compatibility.

t_2a2bc054478b.overview: Living quietly back on the pachinko planet, Pachio-kun gets an urgent call from the Pachinko King: pachinko is losing popularity, so he must head to Earth at once and carry out the Pachinko Land project. Clearing each of the 15 parlors earns part of the blueprint for Pachinko Land, and once every map piece is collected the panels are slid into place like a 15 puzzle, with the moves allowed tied to the machines emptied. Parlors are entered from a map screen; inside, conversations yield bonuses such as a fixed shooting technique and reach patterns, some shops have several floors and hidden rooms, and a magnifier shows the nails. Machines come in paired designs such as Ninja and Monster or Dice and Esper. Running out of balls draws a scolding from the King, and three battery-backed record books keep progress.

t_2a7c0411f5e7.overview: Part of the common 8-bit software found on educational computers, Zhili Pintu, also known as Play Toy Pictures, Caucigrama and Puzzle, is a slide puzzle with 15 pictures to reassemble. Several puzzles use unlicensed artwork of well-known cartoon and comic characters, such as a blue Garfield sitting next to a green Speedy Gonzales without his sombrero; other borrowed characters include The Hulk, the Road Runner, Mickey Mouse and Jiminy Cricket. A later VT01 hack released under the name Puzzle, apparently developed by Inventor, replaces every puzzle design from the original.

t_2ada1236d76b.overview: A family of adventurers takes on an underground labyrinth in this action role-playing game. The family seeks to destroy an ancient dragon sealed inside a painting, which first requires recovering a sword guarded by four hidden crowns. Members of the household, including the father Xemn, his wife Meyna, their children and the family pet, are sent into the vast cavern one at a time, facing traps, puzzles and monsters. Each character differs in attack power, range, jumping ability and usable items, and no single member can use every item. Attacking uses up the character's magic power. The dungeon is laid out four rooms across and sixteen levels deep, with each room scrolling horizontally across four screens.

t_2b5d6cc3b808.overview: Departing from the run-and-gun action of the earlier entries, Ikari III turns the series into an overhead beat 'em up. Two commandos set out to rescue a kidnapped hostage held by the terrorist group Crime Ghost, and they start without firearms, fighting with punches, kicks, jump kicks and roundhouse kicks; machine guns can be picked up from enemies along the way. A life meter lets them survive blows, but gunfire and grenades cost a life immediately. The home version keeps the arcade game's core play with reworked stage layouts and anime-style character designs, has vehicle bosses fought with unlimited-ammunition machine guns, and adds an exclusive fourth stage played as a side-scrolling underwater shooter with the heroes in scuba gear.

t_2b78996e167b.overview: Sybok, a charismatic Vulcan cult leader, has disrupted the peace process on the neutral planet Nimbus III, and this cancelled Bandai action game survives as a four-stage prototype that hands control to one Enterprise crewman at a time. The first stage has Sulu running and gunning through Sybok's followers to free hostages in Paradise City. Next, Scotty works through a more open level, collecting bombs from certain enemies to blow open a door and reach Kirk, Spock and McCoy; rocket boots are needed to climb back out of one section. The third stage flies the Enterprise through asteroids and then against a bird of prey, and the last sends Kirk across the creation planet toward a boss fight with the god creature.

t_2b807f19c02d.overview: Batman heads for the Joker's hideout after the villain steals a set of metals, one of them highly toxic, in this side-scrolling run and gun platformer. The pursuit runs through seven stages, most split into two sub-levels plus boss levels, taking in the Gotham City cathedral, the Joker's warehouse, a snowy mountain, a refinery, an underground conduit, an ammunition base and the Island of Ha-Hacienda. Batman fires a wrist projector whose ammunition changes with collected icons: a crossbow that makes enemies explode, Batarangs that follow enemies, criss-crossing Sonic Neutralizers and spreading Shield Stars. Sliding can also attack some enemies, and collecting eight energy capsules grants a few seconds of invincibility. Three lives come with unlimited continues, and stage passwords are available from the pause menu.

t_2bbe88c1cee8.overview:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles puts a single participant in control of four brothers across action-platform missions. Players navigate five adventure levels from an overhead perspective, entering sewers and buildings that transition to side-scrolling navigation. Guiding Leonardo, Michaelangelo, Donatello, or Raphael, the player can swap members through an information screen. Each character utilizes a signature primary weapon with distinct reach, speed, and attack power to combat the Foot Clan. A turtle whose life runs out is captured until rescued, and the game ends if all four are captured.

Throughout the journey, players collect pizza to recover life and acquire secondary armaments such as shurikens, boomerangs, and Kiai scrolls. Side-scrolling areas involve jumping, ducking, and fighting adversaries, alongside completing goals such as disarming underwater bombs. Later rooftops require ropes to cross gaps. Boss confrontations conclude most levels, culminating in an assault on the Technodrome and a final battle against Shredder.

t_2bf2b322b3bb.overview: Loosely based on the comic travelogue by Jippensha Ikku about two pilgrims on the Tōkaidō, this command-selection adventure follows Yaji and his partner Kita. After a furious quarrel with his fiancée over who runs the household, Yaji announces a pilgrimage to Ise and dashes off down the road with Kita. Each stop along the way presents its own incident to resolve, from a dispute with a gang over redevelopment to a ferry murder mystery, while a larger threat looms in the ghost of a warlord who means to return to power. Fortune-tellers provide hints, and some events only trigger after a reading. A poet teaches a haiku that serves as the password for continuing, and the final Kyoto scenario branches into four different stories depending on the player's actions.

t_2bfc0cf76d60.overview: Played across a table, this head-to-head action game is built around an original ball sport called Dojiball, with ten balls thrown back and forth between the penguin and an animal opponent. A set is won by sending all ten balls to the other side, or by holding fewer when time runs out. A ball that strikes a player knocks him out for a while, and a stunned player can mash the buttons to recover sooner. An obstacle moves across the table later in each set to block the balls, and if the sides are level at time-up, an eleventh ball of a different color is added for a 30-second playoff and bursts on the side where it stays too long. Matches are best of three sets. On the Famicom the first round is always against the computer, later matches between players use the first and second controllers, and names of up to three letters can be entered.

t_2bfea790c90f.overview: Hwang Shinwei made this 1988 Famicom reimagining of Namco's arcade games Rally-X and New Rally-X, which circulated under several titles including Mihun Che and BB Car. The player drives around a giant maze collecting flags while avoiding other cars until every flag has been collected. Trails dropped behind the car make pursuing enemies spin out, but fuel is limited and runs down faster while trails are dropped. Unlike the original, the car can move diagonally, and the computer cars are faster and far more aggressive, constantly targeting the player's exact location. The trail type changes from stage to stage, and the bonus stages of the original are absent.

t_2c04bd8b5194.overview: A young hero sets out to gather seven herbs needed to cure a king of an illness in this side-scrolling platformer, whose lead character is based on the child actor Kenji Sagara, known for his impersonation of baseball player Masayuki Kakefu. Besides jumping, crouching and stomping on enemies, the hero can break into a sudden sprint, brake to an abrupt stop and skip across the surface of water. A small red creature called Wicky can be carried and thrown to eliminate enemies. The game gradually shifts from day to night as a timer counts down, and the ending depends on how quickly the quest is completed: taking more than three hours means the king has died, while faster finishes bring greater rewards.

t_2c0539bd41a9.overview: Loosely based on the folktale Taketori Monogatari, the Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, this adventure is the 1988 Famicom adaptation of the computer text adventure Shin Taketori Monogatari, first released in 1984 for machines such as the FM-7. The goal is to find Princess Kaguya. Where the computer original required commands typed in katakana, romaji or English, the Famicom version replaces them with a conventional menu of selectable commands. In the original design the player chooses the hero's gender at the start, a choice that affects later story developments, and the adventure also offers three difficulty levels, a score of up to 160 points based on the player's inputs, and multiple endings. The story includes some mildly risque humor without being an adult game.

t_2c218c735ce5.overview: Searching for lost children who have been kidnapped by monsters, Sanrio's frog Keroppi sets out on a new adventure in this platform game. Play centers on moving through each level and dealing with the enemies along the way, either by jumping on them or by defeating them with Keroppi's croak weapon. Levels range from the forest to a seaside setting. Bonus levels interrupt the action with a memory challenge in which characters from the Sanrio franchise must be matched in a format similar to the card game Concentration. The game is designed for a single player.

t_2c624bf62453.overview: Dragon Co.'s first known release, programmed by TomSoft Studio, draws loosely on both The Lion King film and the animated spinoff The Lion King's Timon & Pumbaa. Before starting, the player picks Simba, Timon or Pumbaa. Simba is the balanced choice, attacking with his claws and able to swim underwater indefinitely. Timon kicks and throws apples and jumps highest, but his attacks are not effective on bosses and an oxygen gauge limits his time underwater. Pumbaa is heavy to control, cannot dive or hold onto cliffs, and rams enemies with the fastest speed. Each level's exit opens only after its boss is found and beaten. Apples add points and hearts restore health, checkpoints are rare, and an extra life comes every 100,000 points. A pause screen and a credit roll are included.

t_2c9c01cd360b.overview:
Nine missions structure the campaign, presenting players with multiple pathway options to either confront or bypass enemy forces across simulated 3D landscapes. The first seven missions each contain three goals, while the eighth contains two and the final mission contains one. As a fighter pilot commanding a fictional F-14VTS aircraft, the player maneuvers through overhead isometric scrolling environments to repel an extraterrestrial invasion.

Hostile invaders have established four ground installations to siphon energy from Earth toward an alien space station capable of vaporizing the planet. The pilot must navigate mountainous terrain, eliminate alien units, and ultimately demolish the ground bases along with the space station. Mission duties include dropping critical provisions to scientists building a Neutron Cannon in underground caverns, rescuing two scientists, engaging in dogfights, and docking with the pilot's own space station to buy weapons.

t_2d20ea563d98.overview: A side-scrolling stealth action game, this port of Sega's arcade game Bonanza Bros. was made by TXC's Micro Genius internal development studio. It flips the original script: instead of stealing artifacts from guarded venues, the policeman must collect stolen artifacts from locations occupied by enemies. There are five stages, each split into four levels, and every level has two floors with artifacts scattered across them; once all are collected, the policeman leaves by entering the right door. Enemies walk in fixed patterns and attack when approached, some shooting projectiles, throwing bombs or fighting bare-handed, and knocked-out enemies recover quickly. Two players can play simultaneously.

t_2d479374a949.overview: Set on Planet Zi after a great upheaval has left the world devastated and many Zoids badly damaged, this strategy simulation puts the player in command of either the Republic or the Dark Army. Each map is won by destroying the enemy's flagship Zoid. There are 16 maps, and clearing the first 15 unlocks the last. Two rule sets are available: a real-time mode with no turns and a turn-based mode in which each turn allows two one-square moves, which may both go to the same unit. Clashes play out as shooting action sequences with a 20-second time limit. Shifting terrain can turn land into sea that blocks ground units, while flying units can cross water at a small cost in health. Maps hold upgrade parts, supply bases for repairs and wild Zoids that can join the army.

t_2d81ceae7ec9.overview:
Athletes representing chosen nations are controlled by players as they engage in rapid button-mashing actions across various athletic events. The World Tournament covers track events such as dashes, a relay, the 110 meter hurdles, and a marathon; field events such as the long jump, javelin throw, triple jump, shot put, and high jump; weightlifting; the vaulting horse; and swimming races. In the marathon, players instead set their runner's speed for each of the course's six legs.

Up to eight human participants can take part in the tournament, each choosing a country to represent. A Training option lets one player practice any event except the marathon, and battery-backed memory saves records to one of two files.

t_2d9c73deeed3.overview: Released by Nintendo in 1983 for the Family Computer, this mahjong game seats one player against a single computer opponent in two-player mahjong. Two people cannot play together, and the turn order is fixed, with the player going first and the CPU second. A game is a half-game of four hands: East 1, East 2, South 1 and South 2. Three difficulty levels are offered. Beginner, aimed at those who have just learned mahjong, deals generous starting hands; Intermediate makes the starting hands a little tougher; and Advanced forces an automatic draw if no win, draw or call is declared within 12 seconds of the computer's discard. Dora come in standard, hidden and kan varieties, and the pause screen shows a cup bearing the words TEA TIME. The game was later made playable inside Animal Crossing.

t_2dd35f6218fb.overview: Released in 1994 by Magicseries Corp. and also titled Leidian Shenlong Zhuan, this unlicensed shoot 'em up is a port of R-Type for the NES and Famicom. It is considerably shorter than R-Type, with four stages instead of eight, and is likely based on the Japanese PC-Engine release of R-Type, which contains only four stages. Many gameplay elements carry over, including the Force power-up, and all of the original enemies and bosses appear with different designs. The player gets three lives and two continues. Graphics and music are cruder versions of the originals, and heavy sprite flicker occurs when the sprite limit is reached. The game ends with the player's ship landing on a base.

t_2e512414887f.overview:
Across a sequence of distinct stages, players control the humanoid warrior toads Rash and Zitz on a mission to defeat the Dark Queen and rescue their captured companions, Pimple and Princess Angelica. Levels incorporate varied formats, including beat 'em up brawling, platforming, descents along suspended cables, obstacle courses, and vehicle rides on the Speed Bike, Jet Turbo and Space Board, as well as a unicycle. Players have a limited number of lives and an energy meter that is replenished by eating flies.

Progression requires defeating enemies and maneuvering through hazards. Standard offensive moves include punches, kicks and a running head-butt, and double-tapping the control pad with the B button gives access to powerful Smash Hits such as the Battletoad Butt and Big Bad Boot. Certain objects, such as the legs of defeated walker enemies, can also be picked up and wielded. Some moves suit particular hazards; the BT Bashing Ball, for example, uproots Saturn Toadtraps and short-circuits the wall-mounted Retro-Blasters.

t_2eb3b1240524.overview:
A devil named Mandora and his monster forces have driven humanity into the ocean depths. Taking control of a fighter craft, the player flies into vertical combat to eliminate opposing aerial forces and ground targets in an effort to reclaim the Earth.

Destroying hangars releases numbered fighter parts that dock directly with the craft. Up to four attachments add weaponry such as double shots, backward shots and a rear barrier, while also shielding the vessel from incoming strikes. Pressing the A button separates the docked parts into a battle formation whose pattern depends on how many parts are attached, and an on-screen counter limits how often formations can be used. When fully assembled with every component, the craft temporarily changes into an invincible Fire Bird. A design mode lets players arrange their own formations by setting part positions and beam directions.

t_2eecb979d2bf.overview: Ugadayka, a title that translates to Guessing, is a word puzzle made in Russia by A. Chudov for the Dendy system. Play follows a hangman-style format in which a hidden word has to be worked out. Four different options set the vocabulary and alphabet in use: Russian words, Russian words written with the Latin alphabet, English words written with the Cyrillic alphabet, and English words. The game is designed for a single player.

t_2f1279e2ce92.overview: Cony Soft built this bootleg fighting game around an unusual roster of 12 playable characters taken from other franchises: Ryu, Chun-Li and Vega from Street Fighter, Mario and Kupa (Bowser), Sonic, Leonardo of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Haggar from Final Fight, Andy, Mai and Laurence from Fatal Fury, and Goku from Dragon Ball. The Street Fighter II and Fatal Fury characters and their stages are reused from Cony's other pirate fighting games, and much of the music is sampled from games such as Street Fighter II, Super Mario World and Sonic the Hedgehog. After a fight won by a human player, a win screen shows the victor in a victory pose with a single quote shared by every character. Options include changing the IRQ, and a long, unskippable intro opens the game.

t_2f16b6904ddf.overview: Bub is sitting in a park with a girl named Judy when one of the Skull Brothers traps her in a bubble and carries her away, and he becomes a bubble dragon to rescue her. Taito's platform game keeps the play of the earlier games in the series largely unchanged, but the blank backgrounds give way to scenery such as trees and sky that changes every ten levels. Holding the B button lets the dragon float upward, and Super Bubbles can trap several enemies at once. New items include clocks that freeze enemies and bottles of wind that create wind bubbles. Three bonus games are reached after defeating a boss or through certain doors, and a two-player mode is also included.

t_2f3e971f8090.overview: A cross-country road race sends drivers across the United States at around 200 miles per hour, covering roughly 2,990 miles from Boston to Los Angeles. In single-player mode, the driver competes against eight computer-controlled cars across the country, while the two-player mode puts both racers in the same car model in different colors for a head-to-head run. All of the rival drivers are fictional. The cars themselves are licensed Chevrolet Corvette ZR-1 sports cars, which gives the European release its name; the same game was later sold in North America with the vehicles redesigned.

t_2f8c605ed275.overview: Two years of junior college life play out on a board, and the winner is whoever ends up happiest. Each player's face and starting values come from a chosen name and the faces of two parents, and an entrance exam score decides which school they enter. A calendar-style roulette moves play through club events, attempts to find a girlfriend, and end-of-term exams that force every player to stop. At graduation, stats, earned credits and the partner's affection are assessed to produce a final happiness score. Alone, a player aims for the highest score; with up to four participants, they compete to see who was happiest.

t_2fb579628019.overview: In the 22nd century, a biohazard outbreak on the space colony L2 cuts off all contact, and Jin, a survivor of the third survey team who was a pilot rather than a fighter, sets out to learn what happened as the Bio Army seizes power and a resistance fights back from the Satellite Base. Konami's role-playing game stages turn-based battles of up to four allies against up to six enemies. Each character's BP capacity is set by the BP tank they carry, and humans and cyborgs have stats swayed by their emotions, while robots have none. The cylindrical colonies L1 and L2 can be crossed along the outer wall with a spacesuit and oxygen tank, and later a factory at the Satellite Base fuses weapons into stronger ones. The cartridge carries the VRC VII sound chip for FM sound.

t_2fd8f9be8253.overview: The last entry in the Igo Shinan series of Go study cartridges again centers on records of professional games, playable as an automatic viewing replay or advanced by hand, along with a playing-strength assessment. Igo Shinan '94 drops the four historical player collections of the previous edition and substitutes four different historical professionals, whose sets range from 10 to 28 games. A modern category of 38 games completes the library of 119 records.

t_2fe94629acce.overview: Turning the Famicom into a karaoke machine, this Korean cartridge developed by Daou Infosys and published by Daewoo comes with an initial selection of 56 songs. Every song can be picked directly from the main menu. The cartridge carries its own sound hardware, a clone of the Yamaha YM2413 chip, and all of the music comes from that chip rather than from the console's own audio. A microphone input feeds the singer's voice in through an analog-to-digital converter, and the unit has a detachable microphone. A special slot on the cartridge accepts song packs that expand the library, some of them holding 40 songs each.

t_303d3bffcc06.overview: Guiding the hero, Paretto-kun, to the goal within a time limit is the aim of this tile puzzle. A cursor moved with the control pad picks a road tile, and the A button swaps it with the single sea tile on the board. Red road tiles cannot be swapped, and tiles turn blue once Paretto-kun passes over them. He must pick up the key before the goal lets him in, and falling into the sea or letting the oil gauge reach zero is an out; oil items add time and bonus items add points. Enemies such as Mokemoke, Fuwafuwa and Mogura cause a miss on contact, while the Pencil and Paint redraw or recolor road tiles. The 50 stages give a password after every five, the B button speeds the hero up, and one or two players can take part.

t_304b4ce0870a.overview:
Somari recreates Sega's 1991 Sega Genesis/Mega Drive game Sonic the Hedgehog on the Family Computer, with Nintendo's mascot Mario taking the lead role in place of Sonic. The side-scrolling platformer follows the quest to defeat Dr. Robotnik, who has converted all the animals of South Island into evil robots. Most areas are drawn from the original game, though some levels are entirely new, and each level has three acts.

Mario can run at high speeds, although play is slightly slower overall, and he can perform the Spin Dash. Gathering 100 golden rings opens the bonus stage at the end of a level, and a hit costs at most three rings. The unauthorized game was developed by the pirate developer Hummer Team, credited in-game as Somari Team.

t_30551de59d3a.overview: Medieval trappings such as kings and castles meet futuristic technology in this turn-based strategy game built around mechs, with armies that mix mechs and more traditional modern military ordnance like tanks. Progress comes by traveling an overworld and selecting a location; victory there requires taking out the enemy's commander robot and then the enemy's base, and defeating enemies sometimes unlocks new weapons. The player's own mech is the commander unit, always controlled directly, and it can be substantially customized with new equipment and appendages before each sortie, though allied units cannot be. Allies can be controlled directly or given commands that dictate their behavior, such as an all-out assault that rushes into combat range, taking cover, or moving to a flanking position.

t_305cb1a41c5e.overview: Dizzy's goal is to return to his friends and family, the Yolkfolk, and the way home depends on solving a series of puzzles in order to obtain a boat. The search takes him through haunted mines and tree villages as well as underwater. Play centers on inventory-based problem solving with a twist: the player cannot pick a particular item to use, and Dizzy simply drops whatever sits at the top of the inventory list. That makes underwater sections risky, since letting go of the snorkel there means instant death. Dizzy has only one life, and a required subquest calls for thirty gold coins to be collected before the adventure can be finished.

t_30af67c70608.overview: Political maneuvering drives this strategy simulation, set on a distant planet that has recently declared independence and must now choose its first leader. The player picks one of four candidates, a war hero, a king, a nobleman or a businessman, and competes against the others for control of the planet. Each character starts with just three colonies out of a possible thirty, and power is built by winning the support of different political factions through bribery, assassination and civil wars. Up to four players can take part.

t_3125ef9ab6a6.overview: Played out across the Civil War, this strategy game lets the player side with either the North or the South and start in any year from 1861 to 1864. A strategic map of the United States is divided into states and territories, and army units move across it, expanding westward into unoccupied territory and clashing with the enemy. Battles are normally resolved in a real-time action sequence, while capturing forts can win an entire state and seizing an enemy train yields its gold. A standard army has six infantry, three cavalry and one cannon, and each cannon can fire only nine times per battle before withdrawing. Missions and battles can be switched off so the game plays more like a board game. Single-player and multiplayer modes are offered.

t_3156c48dc16b.overview: Considered a parody of the Castlevania series, this platform game stars Kid Dracula, the self-proclaimed Demon King, who wakes from a sleep of ten thousand years only to discover that the demon Galamoth, who has conquered the world, has challenged him. Kid Dracula leaves his castle and battles through nine side-scrolling stages, attacking with magic shots. Clearing a stage powers up those shots and adds new charged-shot abilities, among them homing shots that track enemies, a transformation into a bat that can fly, freezing shots that stop enemies for a time, and an upside-down mode for walking along ceilings for five seconds. Defeating enemies with charged shots yields coins, and a minigame after each stage awards extra lives when won.

t_31c283b73d21.overview: Parasols replace bubbles in this platform game starring Bubby and Bobby, who keep their human form. The parasol works as a shield and a weapon: it can stun enemies, capture droplets or hurl enemies, so weaker foes can be stunned, juggled and thrown across the screen into other enemies. Five captured droplets merge into a large drop with an elemental attack, where water floods downward through the stage, fire sets flames along the ground, lightning sends a bolt across the screen and star fires a spiral of stars. Eight themed planets each hold six stages and a boss battle, and the final foe is Chaostikhan, responsible for stealing color from the worlds. The NES version by Ocean leaves out the extra world of the computer versions.

t_31dba6902350.overview: Based on a Chinese television series about Judge Bao, the platform game does not put the judge himself under the player's control; instead one or two players guide Bao's servants (Gongsun Ce), depending on whether the two-player hotseat mode is selected. Pressing Select summons Judge Bao's secretary Zhan Zhao to clear the enemies on screen. Each world is split into three levels, two built mainly around platforming and the third a boss stage. The mechanics closely follow those of The Dragon, and the title screen music is a rendition of the opening theme of a television series on the same subject.

t_31f6838e0264.overview:
Defeating the eight robots that Dr. Cossack has sent to destroy Mega Man is the main goal confronting the player. Controlling Mega Man, the player navigates eight stages selected in any sequence. The character runs, jumps, slides, shoots, and climbs past obstacles and enemies before facing a Robot Master at the conclusion of every stage. Conquering each boss adds that Robot Master's signature weapon to the player's arsenal. Eliminating all eight Robot Masters unlocks two separate sets of linear stages needed to finish the game.

Mega Man utilizes an upgraded arm cannon that charges energy to unleash larger and more damaging blasts. Traversal support comes from the dog Rush, who transforms into three modes, alongside hidden adaptors found within stages. At designated points in certain levels, Dr. Light's robotic suitcase Flip-Top tosses Mega Man a power-up item.

t_322e5b35656a.overview: Prince Myer of the Willner Kingdom learns that Rubas, the Devil of Darkness, plans to use seven magic bells to summon an army of monsters, and sets out to stop him. Starting outside Rubas's palace, the prince must climb seven bell towers, defeat the boss at the top of each, and burn every bell in the sacred flame, which also destroys its tower; once all seven are gone, the way opens to the final battle. Viewed in an oblique perspective, the nonlinear action role-playing game has Myer walking in eight directions and attacking by throwing a sword. Coins dropped by monsters buy equipment at shops, while hidden dungeons, invisible portals to the Parallel Zones and secret rooms hold stronger gear. Falling off a ledge or running out of life ends the game.

t_3281ce99235b.overview:
Players manage resources to assemble an effective military, cultivate a productive economy for civil and military growth, and maintain peasant respect and loyalty. Most commands are carried out by appointed samurai retainers. The map covers 38 fiefs of feudal Japan, and unifying the country requires conquering all of them, starting from one of two scenarios that begin in 1560 and 1582.

Play progresses through monthly turns on the map. In battle, field warfare allows orders in the morning, afternoon and evening, while siege warfare allows one order per unit each day. Several methods lead to victory in conflict, including eliminating the opposing command unit, compelling adversaries to withdraw, withstanding an attacking army for a month, or extending engagements until enemy supplies run out.

t_3290eaf7ff62.overview: Played from an isometric perspective, this puzzle adventure follows the wizard Shadax into the fortress Kâstleröck after Morbius the Malevolent kidnaps Eleanor, Princess of Arcadia. To stop Morbius, Shadax must gather the six pieces of the Staff of Demnos, which was broken apart and made invisible. The setting is non-linear and consists of 250 rooms, each with a particular puzzle to solve, using hazards such as floors covered in spikes and conveyor belts alongside enemies and movable objects. Some rooms require one of four hidden magic keys, and bombs can be detonated to open blocked passages. Potions grant temporary invincibility, destroy all moving objects in a room or freeze time, blue pointed hats give extra lives, and a map records every room entered.

t_32cc7a4337f1.overview: Played on a dance mat, GLK Dance is a common variant of the plug-and-play game Hot Dance 2000, which runs on Famicom hardware and is loosely based on Dance Dance Revolution. GLK stands for Gold Leopard King; this release uses the same menu system as Revolution 2000 and shows FengLi branding on its title screen. The player hits arrows that scroll to the top of the screen in time with 8-bit renditions of songs, with the up and down arrow positions switched compared with Dance Dance Revolution. Charts include left/right and up/down combinations, which can be performed because the games were sold for dance mats. Variants of the series differ in menus, engine updates and song rosters.

t_32d29634c4ba.overview:
Rescuing a kidnapped teammate named Gadget and defeating the villainous Fat Cat forms the central goal of this platforming adventure. Players start out searching for a missing kitten before working through a series of zones to reach the antagonist's casino and ultimate hideout. In each side-scrolling stage, the chipmunk protagonists traverse environments by walking, jumping, ducking, and collecting objects such as crates and balls to toss at adversaries and end-level bosses. Each hero starts with three hearts and loses one with every hit.

Assistance arrives from fellow Rescue Rangers during the journey. Monterey Jack helps find secret doors and pathways, Zipper keeps the heroes from harm when he flies ahead, and Gadget leaves inventions and clues. In addition to a single-player mode, the adventure offers cooperative two-player gameplay, with one player as Chip and the other as Dale.

t_335c9cc0c0c0.overview: The seventh Super Cartridge collects four games on one menu, one developed by Joy Van and three by Sachen. Sidewinder, the Joy Van title, is a vertical shooter included in its Chinese version. Happy Pairs is a mahjong solitaire game, Tasac is a vertical space shooter, and Silver Eagle is an action game. Each game is selected from the cartridge's menu and played on its own. As with the rest of the series, previously released Sachen games on the compilation had their copyright years removed.

t_3388e6836030.overview: The life of Genghis Khan and the rise and fall of his empire form the backdrop for this historical strategy simulation, whose goal is to unify the whole continent. Building on the system of its predecessor, the third entry in the series adds cultural spheres and climate: eight cultural regions shape economic growth and decide which troop types can be raised, while eight climate zones govern food production and disasters such as typhoons, sandstorms and cold waves. Personnel matters weigh more heavily, with political advisers introduced and directly governed territories removed, and abilities are graded from A to E. Warfare is split into marching and unit battles. Four scenarios run from unifying the steppe in 1184 to the founding of a new dynasty in 1271, and courting consorts produces heirs and blood-related generals. On this cartridge the opening is reduced to the title screen alone.

t_33aa973b2797.overview: A third army, the Yellow Army, joins the war in the fourth strategy entry of the series, and up to three players can take part. A new campaign mode runs through 35 stages in order, each recreating a scene from the original anime. Units now consist of four mobile suits, and command-style battles happen only when famous pilots meet; units led by nameless pilots settle combat through a simplified volley of fire. Famous pilots each have their own levels and stats and grow into stronger pilots as they gain experience.

t_33ba4b89d66e.overview: Racing against the clock, the player guides an Antarctic penguin to the research stations of various countries on the continent. Each station must be reached before time runs out, while the penguin avoids sea lions and breaks in the ice along the route. Fish occasionally jump out of ice holes and can be caught for bonus points, and collecting flags along the way raises the score. The penguin can never die; running out of time is the only way to fail. When the last station is reached, the game starts again from the first level with increased difficulty.

t_33bbc3f8e310.overview: Second-grade arithmetic covers addition, subtraction and multiplication across four games. In a dungeon exploration game, meeting an enemy brings up a problem, and finding the treasure hidden somewhere on the map opens the way to the next stage. A golf game ties sums and differences to shot distances, finishes a hole when the ball drops into the cup, and scores by fewest strokes, with a one-stroke penalty for each wrong answer. Multiplication is practiced by assembling robots on a production line and in a whack-a-mole game on a ten-by-ten grid of multipliers. Instead of lives, health drains over time and with wrong answers, recovers when a stage is cleared, and ends the game at zero. Two courses vary the challenge, for instance by showing or hiding the equation.

t_33cc1f4f019f.overview: Strip mahjong is the theme of this one-player Sachen release. The player chooses to compete against any of four available female opponents and plays mahjong against her. Every time a game is won, the opponent removes a piece of clothing, and an opponent who runs out of money is left fully undressed. The game also carries the alternate title Mahjong Partner.

t_33d151ad8f71.overview: Two fairies, Tam and Rit, climb a monster-filled tower to rescue their trapped mother. Each fairy is armed with a magic rod that does not kill enemies directly: a hit leaves a monster immobilized and crying, and the rod can then grasp it in a magic force-field and smash it against the ground. One or two players can take part. In the arcade original the fairies can never jump and must use ladders, but this Famicom adaptation makes jumping available through an option setting and lets a stomped enemy be paralyzed for a moment. It also adds new scrolling platform stages before certain boss fights, moves one boss battle underwater and gives the presentation a darker tone, while omitting the arcade game's second scenario.

t_33ec89036ed9.overview: Four heroes, each from a different race, are offered at the start of this real-time role-playing game: the Minos are warriors relying on swords and limited magic, the Aylex are primarily magic users best used at a distance, the Dionea are a female archer class, and the Viskam both fight and use magic without excelling at either. The goal is to defeat the evil demon Baal. The King first tests the hero by sending them into the dungeon beneath the castle to find a group of important quest objects; after completing it, the protagonist becomes the Hero of God and explores the rest of the continent for magical scrolls and, eventually, special God-like equipment. Combat takes place in real time without screen transitions, and enemies move only when the player does. Each hero has a unique ending.

t_3408b0f7b0c6.overview: Sunsoft developed and published this Famicom version of the arcade shooting game, in which Opa-Opa, a sentient spaceship, fights off an enemy invasion across the planets of the Fantasy Zone. Each of the first seven rounds holds eight enemy bases; destroying them all brings out the stage boss, and the eighth round is a rematch against every earlier boss in succession before the final boss. Opa-Opa attacks with a standard weapon and bombs, can sprout feet to land and walk on the ground, and spends money earned from enemies, bases and bosses at a shop reached by touching a marked balloon, where prices rise with each purchase. The screen scrolls vertically as well as horizontally, the bases move, a radar shows where they are, and the background disappears during boss fights.

t_340e5d9904d2.overview: Politics and four-player mahjong meet in a game offering two modes. In the leadership race, the player picks one of seven candidates and fights through mahjong to become president of the Minji Party; collecting points takes votes away from other lawmakers, and gathering 270 or more votes leads to a deciding match against three party elders. The elimination mode sets the player against 20 politicians, including opposition party leaders, across 10 rounds. Through the eighth round a first- or second-place finish is enough to advance, but the final two rounds must be won outright. Calls such as pon and ron, along with spoken lines, are reproduced with speech synthesis. A single human player takes part, facing computer opponents at the table.

t_342908c98007.overview: Shredder has kidnapped April O'Neil and seized the Life Transformer Gun, a weapon that could return Splinter to human form, and the turtles set out to stop him. Play starts with Leonardo, but any of the other turtles can be selected from the information screen. Missions are navigated on an overhead map, and entering a sewer or building switches the action to a side-scrolling view. Pizza restores health, and alternate weapons are occasionally dropped by enemies or found in limited quantities. A turtle who runs out of health is captured by the Foot Clan and held elsewhere. The pursuit leads past Bebop and Rocksteady and ends in the reactor of the Technodrome, where the turtles face Shredder.

t_3437934dc1bb.overview: A licensed Japanese release of the American Sammy cartridge Ultimate Basketball, this five-on-five sports game was brought to Japan under the Taito name. The player picks one of seven teams and directs a full lineup of five players on the court, although only one player is under direct control at any moment. None of the athletes are real: every player on the rosters is fictional, and so are their statistics. Fouls matter, and enough players can foul out that only three or four remain on the floor near the end of a game. Two modes are offered, a single game and a championship, and winning the championship in the Japanese version brings a cheerleader over to kiss the winning player.

t_343b458574eb.overview: Bruce Lee stars in this mix of platform action, beat 'em up and one-on-one fighting, released by Ramar International for the Famicom in 1995 with English and Arabic language options. Each level is split into a platforming action section and a fighting section that share the same controls. Lee uses the sprites of Liu Kang, and the end-of-level bosses are renamed characters from the first Mortal Kombat: Scorpion as Suzuki, Johnny Cage as Ram, Kano as Tat, Sonya as Alice Yang and Raiden as Fatek. Text screens before and after each level loosely refer to Bruce Lee's films. Besides the main story mode, a Battle option lets the player fight any of the five bosses in a best two-out-of-three match. Only one player can take part, and Lee is the only playable character.

t_34629392d90e.overview:
Retrieving the sacred Disks of Mishakal from the ruined city of Xak Tsaroth forms the ultimate goal, requiring a confrontation with the black dragon Khisanth. A single player leads an adventuring party through this fantasy setting within a side-scrolling action format.

The lead character is the only party member that moves and attacks on screen, though fallen heroes leave their bodies behind. Rather than remaining passive reserves, all four front-rank companions can sustain damage from hostile strikes, and heroes can be swapped into the lead position via menu options. Individual adventurers utilize varied abilities based on role-playing statistics, ranging from close combat weaponry and ranged bows to defensive healing spells and offensive wizard magic.

t_3495b40c16f8.overview: Turn-based war strategy pits two nations, Red Star and Blue Moon, against each other across a series of maps. Each turn brings a set amount of funds for building units at factories, seaports and airports, and conquering cities near a side's headquarters adds income. The roster holds sixteen unit types: ten land units, two of them foot soldiers, plus four air and two sea units, each with different strengths. Only foot soldiers can conquer cities, which then serve to repair and refuel damaged units. A stage is won by capturing the enemy headquarters or destroying all remaining enemy units in one turn. Fifteen maps are open from the start, two secret maps depend on the nation fought for against the computer, and either side can be assigned to a human player.

t_34c21588d70f.overview: Based on the 1997 film Titanic, this unlicensed beat 'em up puts Jack and Rose under player control as they fight their way through the Titanic, beating up everyone they meet. The film's setup frames the adventure: Jack Dawson wins a trip on the RMS Titanic in a dockside card game and spots Rose DeWitt Bukater, a society girl on her way to Philadelphia to marry her rich fiance Caledon Hockley, who feels trapped until Jack rescues her. Developed by Hummer Team, the game is a single-player brawler with no cooperative mode.

t_34e3a497d3e2.overview: Following the events of Bubble Bobble, Bubby and Bobby set out to defeat the Dark Shadow and rescue the Rainbow Islands, a chain of islands that each have a different theme. Instead of bubbles, the heroes release rainbows that act as weapons, makeshift platforms and item collectors; when jumped upon, a rainbow falls, beating any enemies below it. In each round the goal is to reach the top before the rising sea level catches up, and collecting seven different-colored small diamonds on an island before finishing the round earns a big diamond. This Japanese version does not follow the arcade layout closely, featuring its own original level designs along with story intermissions.

t_35416364c121.overview: Aerobic dance comes to the Family Trainer mat in this music game, where the player follows the motions of an on-screen instructor by stepping on the appropriate buttons across eight classes. In the normal mode, the score begins at 100 and falls by 10 with each mistake. Three modes are available in all: besides the classes, an aerobics mode lets the player keep dancing after failing a song, with no level progression, and a pad mode includes a tune-up option that disables the two central buttons so that melodies can be composed on the surrounding pads.

t_35526306d6a0.overview: Three scenarios drawn from episodes of the Oishinbo manga make up this command-selection text adventure. In the first, the hero boasts to self-styled cultured gourmets that he will serve them something tastier than foie gras; in the second, he searches for a restaurant to soothe a patron angered at being taken to a bad one; in the third, that same patron asks him to rebuild a ramen shop. Food snobs debate the merits of dishes to renditions of classical music, keeping the manga's wry humor. The 15 command types include odd choices such as chanting a spell, lying and acting foolish, and chanting a spell can even lead to arrest and a game over. A password continue system lets play resume.

t_3665c5f19a6a.overview: An isometric action and puzzle game, Airball casts the player as someone an evil wizard has transformed into a ball, who must explore a castle fetching items to solve puzzles. A bar gauge at the bottom of the screen shows the ball's air level. Inflating stations scattered through the arenas refill it and also act as checkpoints, but remaining atop one for too long makes the ball burst. Movement uses the directional buttons and a jump button, and jumping lets the ball ascend stairs. Spikes and other obstacles burst the ball on contact, while gems that appear randomly in rooms are collected for points. The NES conversion, developed by Novotrade for Tengen, was cancelled and survives as prototypes; an early build prompts the player to get the spellbook at the title screen.

t_36d5bf2d0d3a.overview: Professional tennis plays out on a quarter-overhead court in the second game of the Moero!! sports series, released overseas as Racket Attack. The score stays on screen at all times. Sixteen different players are available, eight male and eight female, each with individual strengths and weaknesses; male players face only other men and female players only other women. Matches can be played on grass, clay or hard courts. The one-player mode represents a tennis tournament, while the two-player mode represents an exhibition match between two human opponents.

t_36d91b1b0e32.overview: Split into two halves with separate story arcs, the sequel divides each half into an adventure segment followed by an RPG dungeon. The first half deals with the resurrection of the civil war general Oda Nobunaga, while the second centers on the confrontation between Kujaku and his twin. Asura, Onimaru and Kou Kaiho, three major characters from the manga, accompany Kujaku on his quest and step in at different moments. The text menu of the earlier game gives way to a series of icons, and one of the major locations is Mt. Koya, where Kujaku's temple is situated.

t_374e9ba8c987.overview: Climbing a cylindrical tower toward the summit, the hero defeats enemies and makes use of the tower's devices along the way in an action puzzle game. The design is adapted from Nebulus, whose ports were also known as Castelian, with the original player character replaced by the snack mascot from the title. In Nebulus the tower turns clockwise or counterclockwise behind the climber, and its ledges either form stairs or are connected by elevators. A bonus stage is included, and play resumes with a password rather than saved data.

t_37861b61eb12.overview: A delinquent schoolgirl armed with a submachine gun sets out to rescue her best friend, kidnapped by an alliance of animal schools and held by a two-headed serpent who rules the sky area. Reaching it means passing through five areas home to a ferocious koala, a monstrous lizard, a baboon, a sea serpent and a giant spider. In this pseudo-3D shooter the heroine runs and flies into the screen, steering up, down, left and right to avoid indestructible obstacles while shooting oncoming enemies. There is no life meter, so any collision or hit is a miss; three misses are allowed, with one more for every 500,000 points. Each of the six stages ends with a boss, cleared by defeating the minor enemies around it. Stereoscopic play is supported through the Famicom 3D System, though the goggles are optional.

t_379fcff0c466.overview: Based on the 1985 Hong Kong film Mr. Vampire, the game casts the player as a kung-fu fighter journeying through eight towns overrun by kyonshi, the hopping corpses of Chinese folklore, with each town ruled by its own boss. Battles are one-on-one: the hero enters homes, temples and other infested places, and a defeated kyonshi bursts into flames, earning the gratitude and a reward from the area's owner. Villagers hand out items such as sacred scrolls, temple priests restore health, and training halls teach new fighting techniques in exchange for scrolls. Clearing certain dangerous buildings yields red orbs; once all three orbs in a village are collected, the village boss can be challenged, and beating it opens the way to the next village. The journey ends in a final confrontation with an evil witch.

t_37b1dc92d87d.overview: Played on a reduced 9 × 9 grid instead of the traditional 19 × 19 board, this Famicom adaptation of the board game Go keeps the computer's analysis manageable and allows a smoother single-player experience. Players can take on the computer, play against another human player, or watch a short tutorial in which ninjas explain the rules and strategy of the game. Several difficulty levels are available, and each sets a different handicap, so that either the human or the computer player starts with one or more stones already on the board. During play, little ninja mascots toss the stones onto the board.

t_37fe654db3bd.overview: In 2501, with humanity spread across the Solar System, a robotic laser cannon built to protect Earth from alien invaders malfunctions on a defense outpost on Pluto and begins destroying planets. Every attempt to trigger the station's self-destruct system has failed, so the player takes control of the M-308 Gunner, the most sophisticated combat mech available, to storm the base and set off the device manually. The defining mechanic is the ability to reverse gravity at will, flipping the mech between floor and ceiling. Six stages of two acts each lead to a boss gauntlet, later stages wrap around the screen, and only one power-up, such as the Power Beam or Shield, can be held at once. This Japanese edition adds a full cinematic introduction, extra dialogue and expanded story elements.

t_381bc6a3cbe3.overview: Captured friends and a captive mermaid drive this exploration platformer. After the Fratelli family escapes from prison, Ma Fratelli leads them in seizing most of the Goonies and a mermaid named Annie, leaving Mikey to slip past the Fratellis and set everyone free. The hideout forms an open, interconnected world of ladders and doors, some of them warps. Stepping through a door switches the view to first-person, where rooms are searched by command for items and hidden captives. Every Goonie rescued extends Mikey's health, and all six must be saved before Annie can be released. Gear ranges from a yo-yo, slingshot and boomerang to bombs and molotov cocktails, along with shoes for higher jumps and greater speed and a diving suit for underwater areas.

t_383802ff199e.overview: Set in the Balkans in the late 19th century, the Japanese release follows the swordsman Sir Julian James Bond and his eagle, Cutlass. A British Museum research team has been slaughtered at newly discovered ruins, and a group led by Ruth Grandier, a bandit known for demon worship, has stolen artifacts that could resurrect demons. The College of Arms sends Bond to stop her. Each of the eight levels is a castle, and clearing one awards a new sword. The first seven castles can be played in any order, but each boss is vulnerable to only one sword, and hints to the order are hidden throughout. The House of Ruth opens only after the others are cleared, and the recovered jewels must then be placed in a particular order. In cooperative play, a second player controls the eagle.

t_383f116f2b8f.overview: A high school brawler named Kunio takes on rival gangs in this side-scrolling beat-'em-up, the home version of the arcade game released abroad as Renegade. The story differs from the arcade: here Kunio sets out to rescue his classmate Hiroshi, who has been abducted by yakuza. Hardware limits reduce the number of enemies on screen, but the Famicom version adds new material, including a fight inside a train before facing Riki on a platform at Shinjuku Station, a motorcycle chase in the second stage, a route choice in the third stage that allows skipping the fight with Misuzu, and a final building whose interior is a maze where previously defeated bosses attack in groups. A lives system is used from the start, and the other bosses include Shinji and Sabu.

t_384300b59fa4.overview: Hacker International's Famicom release reworks Menace Beach, the skateboarding side-scroller from Color Dreams, and little of the gameplay is changed. Instead of a boy, the lead character is a woman in a skirt who rides through the stages on a skateboard, using objects found along the way, such as balloons, frogs, bombs and bottles, to defeat enemies. The music and some graphics, enemies and level backgrounds were changed, and eroge images appear between levels in place of the original story scenes. The final boss, Demon Dan in the original, becomes a doctor shooting a syringe. Despite the title and label artwork, Princess Peach does not appear.

t_3860abcf6b13.overview: Codemasters built this maze driving game in the mold of Rally-X. One or two players pilot buggies around dangerous mazes that are filled with renegade buggies, and the goal in each maze is to collect all of the bombs, which is the only way to escape it. The game was also produced for several home computers, and on the NES it formed part of the Quattro Arcade multicart, sharing the cartridge with CJ's Elephant Antics, a platformer; F16 Renegade, a shoot-em-up; and Go! Dizzy Go!, a platformer from the Dizzy series.

t_3879767e8eaa.overview: Seven heroes from manga then running in Weekly Shōnen Jump star in this role-playing adventure, and any one of them can be chosen at the start: Son Goku, Jotaro Kujo, Tar-chan, Momotaro Tsurugi, Ryotsu Kankichi, Tarurūto or Maeda Taison. The chosen hero sets out from a home area, and the areas are linked in a ring; gathering all seven heroes opens the way to the full adventure. Battles use a turn-based tactical system on a field shaped by the surrounding terrain or dungeon walls, with attack, defend, item and special-technique commands and movement ranges that differ by character. Up to three heroes travel together while the rest train at a training hall and still gain levels. The final enemy is an original villain who seeks to cover the world in darkness.

t_388a7c910b0a.overview: Aimed at fourth-grade arithmetic, this educational cartridge from Tokyo Shoseki teaches four topics: division, adding and subtracting decimals, adding and subtracting fractions, and multiplying and dividing decimals, each presented as a minigame. In the division and decimal addition and subtraction games, the player controls a man who destroys monsters inside a dungeon with a sword while an unbeatable ghost runs outside the building, and touching a wrong answer instantly costs a life. Another challenge has the player steer a race car through a complex labyrinth, finding the exit tile while avoiding rival drivers in order to reach the next math question. Every minigame has two difficulty levels, and two players can take turns.

t_38a67593f554.overview: Air hockey against a cast of alien and human regulars is the substance of this Famicom adaptation of a Broderbund computer game. The player and a computer opponent stand at opposite ends of a table and use paddles to knock a puck back and forth; each puck driven past the opposing paddle scores a point, shown by the glass shield at that end shattering, and the first side to reach a set score, usually 15, wins. The Famicom version frames the matches with a story: an inter-galactic salesman whose spaceship has broken down stops at the nearest place for miles, a café, to use the telephone, and the regulars there will not let him reach it until he has beaten them all. Matches can be played as a tournament against the café's visitors or as practice against a single opponent to learn that opponent's weaknesses.

t_38b0823a75c1.overview: Takeda Shingen's campaign to unify the country drives this historical strategy game, which is split into three scenarios. The first, beginning in November 1541, is territory management: commands are issued once a month, normally only in the province where Shingen is present, although a strategist command extends orders to up to three other provinces. The thirteen provinces of the Shinetsu region must be conquered by November 1601, or Shingen dies of old age and the game ends. The second scenario stages the Battle of Kawanakajima against Uesugi Kenshin as seven bouts between seven units per side, and winning the majority advances play to the Battle of Sekigahara against Oda Nobunaga, where surviving troops can be sent as reinforcements. In battle, cavalry, musketeers, archers, spearmen and foot soldiers move in a fixed order.

t_38d8279b354f.overview: Two rebel commandos, Che Guevara and Fidel Castro, raid a Caribbean island to free it from the rule of a tyrannical dictator in SNK's Famicom version of its arcade run-and-gun game. The story is based on the exploits of the revolutionary Guevara and the defeat of the Batista regime in Cuba in the late 1950s. Along the way the two fight off hordes of enemy soldiers, collect weapons dropped by troopers and take control of tanks. Hostages must be rescued rather than caught in the crossfire, since killing them brings large score reductions. Two players can fight simultaneously, and continues are unlimited.

t_390d57a8f929.overview: The arcade brawler Bad Dudes Vs. DragonNinja from Data East reached the Famicom as this side-scrolling beat-'em-up, ported by Data East and released in Japan by Namco. The President has been abducted by the evil Dragon Ninja, and the rescue mission ends in an underground factory where he is held. The hero starts with basic punches, kicks and jumps. Where the arcade game lets two players fight side by side at once, the 8-bit versions offer two-player play only in alternation. The Japanese release has its own title screen, and its ending shows only The End at the White House scene, without credits.

t_3935eea81a61.overview: A construction worker named Harry takes up a giant hammer after the Rusty Nail Corporation tears down his home. Adapted from the arcade original, this side-scrolling platform action game sends him through five levels of enemies and boss battles. The hammer has a large reach: Harry can pound the ground to stun enemies or hold it aloft as a shield. Four kinds of power-ups appear along the way. POW icons give him a comically huge hammer, chili peppers grant a 360-degree swing, hard hats absorb one hit, and a medicine bottle restores one bar of health. Unlike the arcade game, this version gives Harry a life bar instead of single-hit deaths, drops the ability to smack boxes around, and rearranges the stage lineup, replacing some arcade stages with new levels.

t_395c817b816b.overview: JaJaMaru returns in a horizontally scrolling action game made up of twenty scenes. Princess Sakura has been carried off by Namazu Dayuu, and JaJaMaru sets out to rescue her. Each scene scrolls only to the right with no backtracking, and it is cleared by reaching the exit at the far right rather than by defeating every enemy. Most items are hidden inside blocks, among them an invisibility potion, a cart that raises speed, super shuriken that pierce enemies, a flashlight that stuns them and bombs that work as traps. Collecting souls earns extra lives. The frog Gamapa-kun is also concealed in a block; once found, JaJaMaru rides it for a time and it eats enemies. After the final scene the game loops back to the first, and it is played by a single player.

t_39a98b803699.overview: Formula One racing modeled on the 1992 season, which Nigel Mansell won, with the player taking on Mansell's role. Races can be run singly, as part of a full Formula One season, or as practice on a particular track. Sixteen tracks are available, each one taking place in a different country. Before each race the car can be set up by changing the transmission, tires and spoilers, and during a race the tires must be switched out at least once in the pit. Mansell also appears as a disembodied head offering racing advice such as "Don't hit the barrels!" and "Straddle the racing line."

t_39aa97261cf8.overview: Adapted from an arcade title of the same name, play closely resembles the Light Cycles portion of the 1982 arcade game Tron. Each competitor moves around a rectangular play area in the four cardinal directions, creating a line behind that other players will crash into. Speed bursts are available, along with the chance to jump once per life, which can provide an escape from a dead end. The console version uses a stage select screen, much like the Mega Man series, on which the player chooses the opponent to face; each of the five initial levels consists of five rounds and features a different gameplay gimmick. Besides solo play against the computer, multiplayer modes support up to four players.

t_39b13deedeae.overview: Based on Osamu Tezuka's Tetsuwan Atom, known outside Japan as Astro Boy, this side-scrolling platform game from Konami and developer Home Data is set in a future where humans and robots live together. When burglars break into Professor Ochanomizu's lab and steal all of his money, Atom sets out to recover it across ten stages. Instead of extra lives, Atom runs on uranium: each stage begins with 300 points that drain every second, and when he is hit by certain enemies, falls into a pit or runs out of time, the professor uses his own uranium to rebuild him. The professor can also be summoned to refill Atom's supply, and the game ends once both run out. Atom can jump, punch and fly for a limited time, and coins collected by jumping over enemies buy items. Puzzle-solving plays a strong part alongside the action.

t_39e5c92699fb.overview: Officially tied to the 1989 live-action film but with a plot that bears little resemblance to its story, this platformer from Sunsoft sends Batman through five levels: the Gotham City Streets, Axis Chemical Plant, Gotham Sewers, Mysterious Laboratory and Gotham Cathedral Belltower. He can perform a wall jump to scale vertical surfaces and wields three projectile weapons, the batarang, batdisk and batpoon, all powered by pellet cartridges. Bosses include Killer Moth, a device called the Machine Intelligence System, Electrocutioner, a machine known as the Dual-Container Alarm, Firebug and finally the Joker. When continuing after having already reached the Joker, the penultimate boss is skipped.

t_3a175085892f.overview:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles puts a single participant in control of four brothers across action-platform missions.
