t_dd6e333abf49.overview: Japanese high school students Akemi Nakajima and Yumiko Shirasagi combat the forces of Lucifer, unleashed by a demon summoning program that Nakajima created. To reach the demon world, the pair enter a vast subterranean labyrinth explored from a first-person perspective, with turn-based battles arising from random encounters. Enemy demons can be talked into joining in exchange for magnetite, money or items; up to seven can be kept at once, with up to four summoned at the same time. Demon attitudes shift with the moon phase. Demons do not level up; instead, stronger ones are created by fusing two allies at a special location. Progress is saved with passwords, and the generals faced along the way include the Minotaur, Medusa and Hecate.

t_dd8adfb03b0f.overview: A command-selection adventure built around the music group TM NETWORK, with a science-fiction plot full of time paradoxes. In 1999, a satellite launched under the SDI program suddenly runs out of control and begins attacking nuclear warheads around the world. The protagonist, a teenage fan of the band who uses a highly advanced computer called MUE, is thrown back in time to the band's recording studio in 1989 and joins the members in trying to stop humanity's destruction. Investigation works in the usual way for adventure games of the era: choosing commands and moving a cursor onto objects to examine them. Progress also requires clearing mini-games such as a 3D maze and a car chase, and small misjudgments or missed story conditions can quickly lead to a game over.

t_ddccc553718f.overview: Blue and orange balls circle endlessly on a network of frictionless rails in this puzzle game, colliding with and passing one another. The aim is to guide every ball into the storage seat of its own color, either by flipping the orange and blue switch points or by knocking balls into each other. White balls also travel the track and can be put to use, while on some stages red balls appear and end the game if an orange or blue ball touches them. Separate buttons switch each color's points and can eject a ball already parked in a storage seat. Once all orange and blue balls are stored, the time taken is shown and play moves to the next stage. Stages can be selected, and the ball speed can be set to slow, normal or fast.

t_df020f3d3f14.overview: Word comes that yokai are appearing across the country and terrible incidents are breaking out in several regions, so the lord asks Jajamaru to investigate, and he travels the islands of Japan in a two-member party with Princess Sakura. The role-playing adventure is divided into four chapters. At first only the first three are open, but play can start from any of them, and clearing all three unlocks the final chapter, which carries over the level and equipment from the last chapter cleared. Jajamaru can use attack magic but has too little magic power to rely on it often, while Sakura specializes in healing magic with high magic power but low defense. Namazu Dayuu turns ally here, piloting a submarine to help with travel over the sea, and an itako in each town gives out passwords for resuming play.

t_df02216f3d93.overview: Visco's boxing game, released elsewhere as World Champ, spans four weight classes and three modes of play. In the single-player ranking game, a boxer alternates between training, where sparring raises speed, stamina, defense or punching power, and ranking bouts against the five top fighters of the current weight class; defeating the champion moves the boxer up to the next class. Stat gains earned along the way are saved with a password. The versus game lets two players square off, and the tournament game places three to eight players in a bracket until one is left; both accept powered-up boxers entered by name and password. The weight classes run from welterweight through middleweight and cruiserweight to heavyweight, with five named fighters in each.

t_df52de4178bf.overview: Building an original team is the headline feature of this 1990 edition of the baseball game. In League mode six of the 12 teams are picked for a pennant race that one to six players can join, and every player on those six teams can be edited for batting, pitching, running and fielding. Game results, standings, team batting average and ERA, individual records and top-ten lists of pitchers and batters are all saved. 1P Play pits one player against the computer with freely chosen teams, and 2P Play is head-to-head; neither allows editing. Pitchers can throw forkballs, changeups, fastballs, curves and shootos to the inside or outside, and they tire and sweat after giving up repeated hits, calling for relief. Fielders can dive and leap, defensive shifts and pickoff throws are available, and certain pitchers and batters have set affinities against each other.

t_df7178bd34f9.overview: Rival spies race each other on a tropical island in this cancelled localization of the Japanese release Nangoku Shirei!! Spy vs. Spy, which Kemco appears to have intended for a 1988 release. The goal is to recover all the vital items and leave before the opponent does. Players search the beaches of the islands for items buried in the sand, assembling a missile from its parts, and the victorious spy escapes the island via a submarine. Traps can be placed in spots where missile parts might be, catching an opponent who comes looking. Compared with the Japanese version, the prototype has a changed title screen, replaces the specific island names with generic nouns, and makes walking faster.

t_df849ae24815.overview: A follow-up to the 1988 racer of the same name, this Famicom sequel returns to circuit racing with car setup options made considerably more detailed than before, so machines can be tuned more finely before heading out on track. Its graphics were also improved over the original. The grand prix mode works differently from a real race weekend, however: qualifying is left out entirely, and the player's car always starts each race from pole position.

t_df9e29714519.overview:
Best of the Best - Championship Karate focuses on the sport of kickboxing. The player starts as the sixteenth-ranked kickboxer in the world and climbs the rankings by winning bouts, collecting trophies and raising the fighter's cash value along the way.

Before a match, the player picks eight blows from more than 32 available strikes, and a training mode raises strength, reflexes, and resistance. One player can face the computer, or two players can fight each other, and passwords save progress. Winning enough bouts earns an invitation to the Kumate, a no-holds-barred fight with no referee.

t_dfa0dd65dfc4.overview:
Guiding Lieutenant Solid Snake, the player infiltrates hostile territory while avoiding detection by guards and surveillance equipment. Snake begins with a combat knife and handgun, using melee strikes, firearms, and planted explosives across locations such as a jungle, a battleship, a train, and a castle. Raising an alarm brings attacking soldiers, requiring the player to defeat the troops or escape them. Knocking out enemies with punches occasionally yields ammunition or rations. Rescuing hostages and interrogating enemy officers with truth gas increases Snake's rank, expanding his health and carrying limits.

Progression requires finding pass cards to unlock doors and using a transceiver to reach three contacts. Exploration shifts between top-down perspectives and side-scrolling sections where Snake walks, jumps, or crawls. In side-view areas, weapons are limited to a knife, handgun, and plastic explosives, with underwater paths requiring oxygen tanks.

t_dfa8b57446b3.overview: Six Sachen puzzle and board games share the sixth Super Cartridge, each launched from a menu. Colorful Dragon has the player control a dragon in a maze that must bite other dragons' tails. Pyramid II is the official sequel to Pyramid, while Pipe 5 is a Pipemania clone and Millionaire a Monopoly clone. Dancing Blocks has the player collect fruit and use the sides of the controlled block to attack, and Locksmith combines exploration and shooting with Rubik-style puzzle solving. All six were developed by Sachen and drawn from its SA-numbered lineup.

t_dfbfa24498fa.overview: Set in 2090 in Lemuria, an isolated cyber-city that became the center of rebuilding after a global catastrophe in 2040, this role-playing game uses first-person, pseudo-3D exploration. A brilliant electronics scientist, branded a heretic because his research had advanced too far, travels a century into the future, and his son Jun boards the same device to follow him. In the future world, an artificial intelligence turns out to be Jun's own creation. Jun's main tool is the Virtual Data Sensor, a visor-type computer worn on the head that at first can use only its online talk system and gains further systems as the adventure progresses, including a combat support system with three types of battle programs.

t_dfcc6305fc22.overview: Based on Akira Miyashita's manga Sakigake!! Otokojuku, this Famicom release is a side-scrolling action game in which the player controls the first-year students led by Momotaro Tsurugi. Each stage is laid with traps and ends with a boss. A jumps, B punches, up plus B kicks, and pressing A and B together spends stamina on a special technique. During scrolling sections, pressing START swaps team members, and a gauge can be spent on a cheer that restores stamina. Rescuing Hidemaro within a stage brings in a new ally, and getting past stage gimmicks raises the team's level and abilities, though these reset at the next stage. Togashi, Toramaru and J are playable from the start, while Raiden, Hien and later Omito Date join as chapters are cleared and fight only in boss battles. Play is single-player.

t_e0048d5dfc1b.overview: Played on an island seen from overhead, this sequel to Dig Dug arms Taizo Hori with two weapons. An air pump inflates enemies until they burst, while a jackhammer used at fault lines on the map creates faults in the ground. When a system of faults divides the island in two, the smaller section sinks into the ocean along with every creature on it, Taizo included if the player is careless, and the points earned depend on how many enemies are taken out at once. The foes are Pookas, round red monsters with goggles that kill on contact, and dragon-like Fygars that can also breathe fire. After three pieces of land have been cut away, a bonus vegetable appears for extra points. When only a few enemies remain, they head for the edge of the island and jump into the water, ending the round.

t_e05244ed3048.overview: Side-scrolling action brings the hero of Power Blade back for a sequel in which the first four buildings can be tackled in any order before Area 5 opens up. In each building the goal is to destroy the boss, which destroys the building itself, and defeating the Area 5 boss leads on to the final level. New to the hero's moves is a slide that lets him travel faster and slip underneath enemy fire. Beating mid-level bosses earns four collectible suits: one lets him climb on walls and ceilings, one lets him swim, one lets him fly, and a defensive suit surrounds him with a rotating shield. The suits share the same powerful energy attack, and although they no longer absorb hits, they drain energy.

t_e07b17a5a0a8.overview: In the original Japanese release of this scrolling shooter from Compile, a shrine maiden summons the Gun-Nac ship and becomes its pilot. Across eight levels the ship takes on hosts of enemies, and collecting a wing enlarges it so that it can survive two hits instead of one and push its weapons further. Five primary weapons, including a flamethrower and a guided boomerang, come from numbered circles, while four kinds of bombs come from lettered ones; picking up matching circles in a row raises a weapon or bomb level, and Power P's add more firepower. Money found during play buys upgrades in a shop between levels. This version keeps the intro, the ending and the first phase of the last boss, which the American release removed or changed.

t_e12448e6741a.overview: In the year 2XXX, the mysterious Planet X appears when Pluto and Neptune switch positions in the Solar System, and its inhabitants attack Earth using a legion of space monsters. Godzilla joins forces with the guardian monster Mothra to repel them. The two monsters take turns moving across a board like chess pieces, where each hexagonal space represents a playable side-scrolling level set in rocky, jungle, city, or hyperspace zones. Moving next to an enemy monster starts a battle with a forty-second time limit but no countdown timer. Foes include Gezora, Moguera, Varan, Hedorah, Baragon, Gigan, and Mechagodzilla, and on Planet X every previous monster returns along with King Ghidorah. Dogora and Manda appear as common enemies throughout.

t_e1429016aecd.overview: When a red star appears in the sky to signal the return of Daimajin, the Dragon Warriors take up the fight again, and after they defeat the Ryu no Kiba and the Gekko-shu, people begin disappearing as the city turns into a demon-controlled zone. The third Culture Brain entry gives each Dragon Warrior a chapter of the story and adopts more realistic character designs. Every character has unique special moves and an independent health bar, and transformed fighters battle with weapons such as swords and staffs. The level-up system of the previous entry is gone, some enemies can deal heavy damage in a single hit, and falling into a pit means instant death. The opposing forces include the Five Great Myo-o, led by Fudo, as well as Red Falcon.

t_e15cdc22bd4c.overview:
Guiding a party of up to six custom characters, the player explores a multi-floor underground maze beneath Trebor's castle. Adventurers are created at the Training Grounds by selecting from five races and three alignments, then distributing bonus points to qualify for one of eight professions. The Fighter, Mage, Cleric, and Thief are joined by the Wizard, Samurai, Lord, and Ninja, which demand higher statistics, while spellcasters draw on seven levels of Mage and Cleric spells.

The party navigates ten maze levels displayed from a first-person perspective, each built on a 20-by-20 grid. Hostile encounters pit the team against one or several groups of monsters to gather experience and gold. Pits, spinners, teleporters, and secret doors are among the hazards. The primary objective is to defeat the Great Wizard Werdna and recover the amulet he stole from Trebor.

t_e17e090ab02a.overview: Tile-clearing puzzles make up Scarabeus, an unreleased NES prototype described as a modified black and white version of the Game Boy puzzle game Pyramids of Ra. Each stage is a series of tiles, and the player must figure out the best path to draw one line through them without any overlap. The tiles crumble away after use, which leaves no choice but to venture on rather than backtrack. To finish a stage, all of the black tiles have to disappear and the player must land back on the starting square, with a reward for a quick performance.

t_e1fdceed9fbc.overview: Gargamel has captured three Smurfs, planning to have them for dinner, and one Smurf sets out to rescue them in this side-scrolling platform game based on the series. The route crosses forests, swamps, mountains and mines, and along the way the hero also rides storks, mine carts and logs. The adventure is divided into ten acts, running from The Forest, The Swamps and The Sarsaparilla Fields through The Old Gold Mine, a sledge race and a bridge before reaching Gargamel's Manor House. Boss fights against Azrael and a dragon punctuate the journey; defeating the first two bosses frees the first two captives, after which Gargamel himself can be confronted. Mushroom and bubble bonus stages also appear.

t_e200d2d124cf.overview: Rather than a finished shooter, Dezaemon is a construction kit for designing a vertically scrolling shooting game of three stages. Users draw the player ship, four kinds of regular enemies with up to four animation patterns per stage, a mid-boss and a stage boss, and assemble backgrounds by combining sixteen 16-by-16 tiles. All graphics and music except the font can be replaced with original work. The music editor offers two melody parts with 24 timbres, a drum part and a fixed triangle-wave part, and six songs can be saved. Finished games use a stock of lives with no life gauge, and the ship's power-up performance cannot be specified. Each 16-by-16 image is limited to a four-color palette including transparency, and songs end after 12 bars.

t_e231316daae5.overview: Fast-paced rail shooting unfolds in a third-person view from behind the hero, Harrier, who travels through a continuous series of stages armed with an underarm jet-propelled laser cannon. The objective is simply to destroy all enemies, and most stages end with a boss that must be killed before moving on. Because of the hardware's display limits, characters are drawn smaller overall than in the arcade game, and some music, boss characters and Harrier's voice were cut; the third-stage boss, for example, became two stone faces that attack several times. The final boss HAYA-OH appears, and the original title-screen and game-over sounds were carried over.

t_e242b36f87f5.overview: In a side-scrolling action game set in the world of Robocco, the player controls a shape-changing robot named R-10 and his human controller, Lance, who battle evil robots in a struggle to liberate the world from evil. R-10's form changes with each kind of mission. On land the robot becomes a train, following the railroad tracks to the boss of the level; when the player must fly to the next mission, it turns into an airplane; and sea missions require transforming into a submarine. The player has three lives and three continues to see the adventure through.

t_e26722a95991.overview: Instead of following the official 8-bit release, this unlicensed cartridge from Super Game is a bootleg port of The Lion King on the Genesis. It plays as a platformer built around the stages of that 16-bit version, though not every stage survives the conversion: the levels "The Stampede", "The Elephant Graveyard" and "Exile" are left out. From "Hakuna Matata" onward, every level of the Genesis game is included, so the later part of the adventure is reproduced in full. The port is a separate production from the official NES version made by Dark Technologies and published by Virgin.

t_e280016a0e6d.overview: Set in a dream world, this side-scrolling action game sends the player to rescue Princess Rua, who has been carried off by an unknown kidnapper. The hero is assembled from a toy box of spare parts: the player picks a face, a body and arms, then gives the character a name. Every part carries weight, and the heavier the total, the more movement speed and jumping power suffer. Eight arm types serve as weapons, among them a parasol, boomerang, shuriken, pencil and melody, and each powers up through five levels. The world map links six destinations, from Starfall Hill and the Milk Sea to Shaved Ice Mountain, the Playing Card Castle and the Fairy Forest, with the routes between them forming 15 stages.

t_e2e98c46d2a2.overview: A spin-off of the Gradius series, this puzzle-platformer stars a sentient moai statue, one of the enemies of the Gradius games, and takes its themes from Easter Island. Each stage is a single screen filled with platforms, enemies and obstacles, and the goal is to rescue the other moai and then escape through a door before the timer expires. The hero can smash certain blocks and enemies with a head-butt and, in some stages, drop bombs to destroy blocks below him. Touching an enemy, falling into a pit, landing on hazards, being crushed by falling objects or running out of time costs a life, while clearing a stage earns an extra one. There are 56 stages, and a password system allows continuing a game.

t_e2fc86bd310b.overview: Adapted from the Kyouryuu Sentai Zyuranger television series, this five-stage action game hands control to a different Ranger in each stage. Play starts with Tiger Ranger and continues in fixed order with Ptera Ranger, Trike Ranger and Mammoth Ranger before finishing with Tyranno Ranger. Every stage ends in a showdown with one of the senior commanders of the enemy organization. Dragon Ranger also appears, but only as a supporting character who cheers the team on from the sidelines; he cannot be controlled in any stage. Published by Angel, the cartridge followed the same publisher's Famicom game based on the previous series, Choujin Sentai Jetman.

t_e2fff7ad9ae3.overview: Side-scrolling action starring Honey Bee, a bee fairy girl who can fly, and Takahashi Genjin, whom she rescues at the end of the first stage; from the second stage onward he becomes the playable character. Unlike Takahashi Meijin no Bouken-jima, the screen can also be scrolled back to the left. Each stage's boss waits behind a castle door at the right end of the action stage, and that door opens only after the correct password letters have been collected in block-breaking segments at eight locations. In those segments, grabbing any letter other than the correct one flashes the screen red and counts as a miss. Clearing all four stages leads to the ending, after which a second loop begins.

t_e352645eb53c.overview: Big Two, the card game known in Chinese as Chu Da D, is the basis of this 1995 Famicom release published by Fortune Power and Jichang. The goal is to win the championship by playing against a lineup of Hong Kong movie actors, among them Jacky Cheung, Stephen Chow and Maggie Cheung. Each stage is split into six levels, and moving on to the next stage requires winning a certain amount of money. The instructions screen lists the hands that can be played, from single cards and pairs up through straights, flushes, full houses, four-of-a-kind and straight flushes; the A button selects cards and B passes. A beginner mode and a harder master mode are available.

t_e3807ad494ef.overview: During an unnamed young girl's birthday, she receives a small green creature named Yumetaro as a gift and is delighted with him. One night her other toys come alive and take the girl to another dimension, and Yumetaro goes after her. The central mechanic is a star that Yumetaro can spawn above the horn on his head: it is necessary for defeating enemies and doubles as a platform that can be ridden to reach otherwise inaccessible areas. The journey spans six stages and six bosses. Each stage hides an area containing a magic item, and collecting all of them without using a continue opens a secret stage with an extra boss. On the cartridge retitled Mr. Gimmick, the player has eight lives instead of the four in the Japanese version.

t_e3980916bbab.overview:
A password feature allows play to resume at a later level. The storyline involves aliens seizing control of a robot-manufacturing planet and reprogramming its robots for war. Players control Low-G-Man, whose jump grows higher as anti-gravity material capsules are collected, from about three-quarters of a screen at the start to about one and three-quarter screens with three capsules. Defeating enemies without freezing them first yields items far more often.

Standard combat relies on the Electro-Magnetic Disruptor Pistol, which freezes targets. Once adversaries are immobilized, the player attacks them from above or below using an extending spear. Additional available weapons comprise fireballs, boomerangs, waves, and bombs. Some enemy vehicles, the Walker, Spider, and Hover, can be captured by freezing them and stabbing the robot driver.

t_e3cbe58d9734.overview:
Burai Fighter tasks the player with shooting robo-mutants, half robot and half living flesh, to stop the Burai's conquest of the universe across seven bases. Controlling an unnamed protagonist equipped with a proton pack, the player floats through two-dimensional space environments. In the side-view levels the screen scrolls in changing directions, requiring the character to avoid getting caught against the screen edges, and a boss waits at the end; in two top-view levels the goal is to destroy the bases. Holding the attack button locks the aiming angle so the player can fire independently of movement. Hidden rooms may contain power-ups.

Beginning with a basic weapon, the protagonist can acquire upgrades such as ring, laser, and missile armaments, and Cobalt Bombs clear the screen of ordinary enemies. Three difficulty settings are available: Eagle, Albatross, and Ace. Higher difficulties feature faster and more aggressive enemies, different adversaries, adjusted bonus multipliers, and alternate endings. Level progression can be resumed using passwords.

t_e3f2b62b6cb2.overview: Mark Greenshields programmed this unfinished NES conversion of Sensible Soccer, using the original Amiga code as a reference. The original game is a football game viewed from a zoomed-out bird's-eye view, built around a simple control scheme and an aftertouch feature that lets shots swerve. On the NES, the footballer sprites and graphics come close to the Amiga original within the console's palette limits, and the menus and in-between screens are all functional. Matches are fully playable, but the build lacks final polish: sound effects are weak, crowd noises and crowd and panel graphics are missing, and the computer opponent needed more work.

t_e4a8585c361e.overview: Tennis for up to four players is on offer in this Home Data production, released by Asmik in Japan and later sold abroad as Top Players' Tennis. In single-player mode, the goal is to compete in the four Grand Slams: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open. Before entering the Grand Slams, a player must first win the qualifying tournament, the Asmik Open. Singles, doubles and mixed doubles matches are all available, and with a multiplayer accessory the game accommodates up to four simultaneous players.

t_e4d0f0f4c906.overview: Idea-Tek developed this beach volleyball game in 1991 as a clone of Kings of the Beach, and several distributors released it, Gluk Video among them; in the United States it appeared as Venice Beach Volleyball. Four teams take part, two made up of men and two made up of women. Alongside the features expected from the sport, a crab randomly comes out of nowhere, steals the ball from the ground, and lets the team that scored the point serve earlier. Matches can be played against computer-controlled teams, or two players can challenge each other head to head.

t_e5082ec63fcf.overview: Hatching and raising a chick is the whole focus of this virtual pet game modeled on the Tamagotchi. Play begins with a choice of a few eggs, which must then be cared for until they hatch. During incubation the player can flip an egg upside down or change the temperature, while a box in the upper-left corner of the screen shows the current weather; letting the temperature sit at the wrong point for the weather ends the attempt and forces a restart from scratch. Once a chick hatches it can be given a name, and a new set of commands appears, with options for giving the hen food and clothes or taking it on an outing.

t_e576804b0cb1.overview:
Seven Levels divide the side-scrolling stages, each with a map screen whose doors lead to stages, bonus games that award extra lives, Museums, and Arenas. Secret switches open warp stages for traveling between Levels. Players guide Kirby across Dream Land to retrieve the fragments of the broken Star Rod and defeat Nightmare. The primary objective requires reaching the end of each stage while preserving a health meter from hazards and adversaries.

Controlling Kirby involves running, jumping, crouching, sliding, and inhaling foes to spit them out as star projectiles. Kirby can also puff up to fly across gaps, releasing an air pellet to drop down and hit enemies. Consuming specific swallowed targets grants special abilities, including firing lasers, using hammers, or bursting into flames. These abilities can open hidden routes, be discarded, or become dislodged upon taking damage.

t_e5b750aeb9c7.overview:
Taking down enemy aircraft that attempt to destroy the player's stealth fighter forms the primary objective in Stealth ATF. Piloting the Stealth Advanced Tactical Fighter, the player manages every phase of flight across missions set in theaters around the world, such as the Middle East, Alaska, and the Pacific. Two players can take turns, and a second player can also take control of an enemy plane for a dogfight.

Gameplay spans launching from a runway, aerial combat, and returning to touch down safely once the engagement concludes. Levels present distinct environments and runway styles, ranging from expansive land strips to compact aircraft carrier decks at sea. While engaging opposing bogeys with onboard cannons and missiles, the pilot must monitor current flight altitude to prevent fatal crashes, while also tracking craft damage levels and remaining munitions. Once per mission, a stealth mode hides the fighter from enemy radar to evade missile attacks.

t_e5b891d19f21.overview:
A kidnapping crisis erupts after the Dragon Ninja abducts the President. Two tough brawlers named Blade and Striker set out across the city to rescue the chief executive from the Dragon Ninja and his henchmen.

Controlling a brawler, the player punches, kicks, and jumps to fend off hostile forces. Ninjas, lady ninjas, samurai, attack dogs, and flaming ninjas attack, some with throwing stars. Players can pick up nunchakus, knives, health items, and time extensions while advancing through locales including city streets, a truck, sewers, a forest, a train, and a cave. Levels conclude with super warrior bosses who must be defeated before a final helicopter confrontation. Multiplayer allows two participants to play by alternating turns.

t_e603eb075582.overview:
A remote-controlled mining robot is guided through subterranean caverns to unearth crystals, blast away terrain, and evade subterranean threats across 100 levels. Navigating dirt, rocks, and expanding pools of mud or lava, the vehicle clears paths by shooting energy blasts or setting explosives gathered from item caches. Boulders can be shoved aside horizontally or dropped onto alien enemies, while certain environmental hazards, such as radioactive stones or hostile creatures, demand cautious maneuvering or heavy demolition.

Completing a level requires gathering a predetermined quota of crystals before the countdown clock expires. Reaching this target reveals a teleportation exit square leading deeper into the planetary crust. Hidden beneath the soil and boulders are power-ups that augment the machine with increased shot range, simultaneous rapid fire, bomb stockpiles, temporary damage shields, and extra lives. Players begin with an allotment of five robots, and the title supports two players.

t_e6129857f7a2.overview: Released in North America as Flying Dragon: The Secret Scroll, this martial arts action game from Culture Brain follows Ryuhi, a Kempo master raised on high mountain tops. After his teacher Juan, author of the Secret Scrolls, is attacked and the scrolls are stolen by the Tusk Soldiers, the dying Juan sends Ryuhi to Shorinji, where the bishop Gengai trains him; he then enters the World Tournament of Contact Sports to stop them. Play alternates between side-scrolling journey levels, in which Ryuhi must defeat bosses and find certain items, and tournament levels of one-on-one fights. Collecting all six scrolls on the first run earns one ending, while the true ending requires a second playthrough in which the six scrolls must be gathered again along with four crystal balls that appear only in that quest.

t_e61bf8565552.overview: Falling-block puzzling moves into three dimensions here, with the view looking down into a rectangular pit. Polycube blocks of various shapes appear one at a time and fall slowly toward the bottom, and each can be rotated around any of the three coordinate axes and moved horizontally and vertically before it settles. Once any part of a block touches the floor of the pit or an already-placed cube, the whole block freezes in place. A solid layer of cubes with no gaps, called a face, disappears and lets the cubes above drop down to fill the space. Blocks fall faster as play continues, and the game ends when they stack up to the top of the pit. The cartridge is a prototype of an unreleased NES port of Blockout.

t_e61ea01f51ea.overview: A Famicom spin-off of the sliding-tile puzzle Blodia, itself based on a computer game called Diablo, this action puzzle game swaps the original rolling ball for cartoon dinosaur-like characters and adds role-playing elements. In Blodia, the playfield is a grid of tiles carrying pieces of track, with a single empty space into which neighboring tiles can be slid. Rearranging the tiles ahead of a moving traveler builds a continuous route, and anything that reaches a tile without track falls out of play. Blodia Land carries that concept over to its own characters while layering role-playing features on top of the puzzle formula.

t_e61fce4ae64a.overview: Four orphans from the village of Ur are chosen by the dying crystals to restore balance to the world as Warriors of Light. The story opens on the Floating Continent, a land hovering above the rest of the planet, and the party explores the world on foot, using a chocobo, by boat and eventually by airship. A job system lets characters switch between classes with unique abilities at any time outside combat, starting from the default Onion Knight class; summoners can call monsters into battle to deal heavy damage, while ninjas can steal. The main antagonist is Xande, another student of Magus Noah, who is creating the flood of darkness to achieve immortality.

t_e6276bd357c2.overview: Set in Japan's Sengoku period, this single-player simulation follows a warlord's campaign to bring the whole country under one rule. Orders are issued season by season, with domestic management used to make the home domain prosperous while war is used to seize new territory. On the battlefield, the player commands generals alongside ashigaru foot soldiers, cavalry, archers, gunners and spearmen. A battle ends when one side's ashigaru and military strength are reduced to zero, when a side retreats, or when the defenders hold out for 30 days. Direct orders can be given only to the player's own domain; vassal states accept just four broad policies: wealthy, military state, normal, or raising rice yield.

t_e63e51c3552b.overview: Three years after his adventures in Ys, Adol Christin and his friend Dogi return to Dogi's hometown of Redmont in the province of Felghana. Lord MacGuire, the King of Felghana, is seeking a set of statues linked to a demon of great power that ruled Felghana long ago, and Adol becomes caught up in the threat facing the town. Instead of the top-down camera view of the earlier games, this installment uses a side-scrolling platformer presentation. Automatic bump attacks are removed, so a button must be pressed to make Adol attack enemies. Spells are represented by rings instead of wand icons, and magic points are renamed Ring Power.

t_e6a85408543f.overview: Firefighting becomes a breakout-style action game in Flying Hero, an arranged Famicom port of Me-Gumi Rescue. Rather than steering the fireman directly, the player moves an assistant holding a net left and right, catching the fireman and bouncing him back up toward the windows of burning buildings. Landing on a burning window puts out part of the fire, and reaching a window with a trapped victim lets him carry that person out, after which the victim must also be caught in the net. Fires spread to neighboring windows over time, faster in later stages, and sparks can burn the net. A stage is cleared once the flames are fully extinguished or every victim has been rescued. Certain items open timed interior screens, and the controller from Arkanoid II is also supported. Play is for one player.

t_e6f28b69882c.overview: Mixing command-selection adventure with role-playing elements, Maharaja sends its hero on a holiday trip to India. On a riverbank he finds a wooden crate, and an old man training nearby explains that it belongs to a maharaja who has been searching for it and who rewards whoever finds it. Exploration proceeds by choosing from a menu of commands, while battles switch to a mode in the style of a role-playing game. Defeating enemies earns experience, and the hero can rise to a maximum level of 30. From level 3 onward, magic chants called mantras can be learned, sixteen in all, and one of the commands is used to cast them. Progress can be saved anywhere except inside the jungle, the tower and the castle.

t_e6f9c66e9108.overview: Prince Lolo journeys through Eggerland to rescue Princess Lala, who has been captured by King Egger. Each room is a grid puzzle in which Lolo must collect every Heart Framer; doing so opens a treasure chest, and taking its contents clears the room. Lolo's only weapon is the Magic Shot, which temporarily turns enemies into eggs that can be pushed but not pulled, and green Emerald Framers can likewise be pushed around freely. The rooms themselves are arranged on a large grid, forming a labyrinth that opens up as rooms are cleared, with some stages hidden.

t_e7641040c4af.overview: Controlling the golden-armored knight Gilgamesh, the player must scale the 60 floors of a tower to rescue the maiden Ki from the demon Druaga, who plans to use an artifact called the Blue Crystal Rod to enslave mankind. Every floor is a maze in which Gilgamesh needs to locate a key and then reach the door that leads upward, fighting the enemies that stand in the way. Each floor also conceals a hidden item that is uncovered only by completing a specific task. Spending too long on a floor sends two indestructible Will-o-Wisps charging toward the knight. This release is the Famicom version as included on an Evercade compilation cartridge.

t_e7addb286ef0.overview: Chengdu Tai Jing Da Dong Computer produced this unlicensed action game around 1994, drawing on the Contra series without copying any single entry. Instead of cloning an existing game, it remakes the engine and uses it in completely different levels. The box text casts Contou as a hero who stands up once again against an alien attack, with a storm of bullets raging over a devastated city. The arsenal behaves differently from the originals: the machine gun fires slower and cannot be used while jumping, the spread gun only fires in three directions, and the laser can put multiple shots on the screen at once. Unresponsive controls and poor programming make it very difficult, and in certain spots the player can occasionally die for no reason.

t_e833dbb2e0dc.overview: Blending a command-based mystery adventure with role-playing and shooting mini-game elements, this 1988 Capcom release unfolds in a fictional professional baseball world. The protagonist, Igawa Suguru, is a former pitcher who retired after a shoulder injury and has been framed for murder. To prove his innocence and uncover the truth, he travels through seven cities, among them Yokohama, Tokyo, Nagoya, Hiroshima and Osaka, while slipping through a police dragnet. Life points drop as he walks; officers who spot him trigger an escape mode, and failing to evade questioning leads to a vertical shooting sequence. Disguise items bought at department stores help with the police. Professional tryouts, passed by clearing three mini-games, are the only way to earn money, and an actual baseball game is also playable.

t_e8b315ea27fe.overview: Alien invaders threaten Earth, and the player pilots Ixpel, a robot that can transform into a jet fighter, on a journey that leads into outer space. In robot form it walks forward and backward and jumps but cannot fly, while the jet can reach any part of the screen; changing forms takes careful timing because no shots can be fired mid-transformation. The jet burns fuel shown on a gauge, and running dry over the ocean means a crash, so the electric spheres found on the ground are needed to refuel. Two weapons are available: the rapid-fire Pulse Laser and the charged Big-Bang cannon, which is the only way to defeat bosses. Stages range from grassland to desert and across the sea, and after the second boss the game loops with altered enemy patterns. Extra lives come at 10,000 and 30,000 points on the Famicom.

t_e8b3541eb3b5.overview: A maze game in the vein of Pacman, The Universe Soldiers from Gamtec has the player drive a car through mazes collecting the dots. There are 50 mazes to complete, and each runs against a timer: the early stages allow more time, while later stages leave less time to finish the maze. Enemies move at different rates of speed, and some change from red to yellow, creating more dots. Power-ups can stop enemies in place, award an extra life, stop the timer, or turn enemies into fruit. Two difficulty modes determine the speed of the car, with the hard setting making it go much faster.

t_e8ba3cb91833.overview: An earthquake has buried all the food underground, and the mole hero must dig through the earth, eat every piece of buried food and then head for the exit door together with his wife. Each stage is a careful puzzle: rocks cannot be moved, and climbing upward is impossible without a ladder, so a single wrong step can leave him stuck with no way forward or back. There are no enemies and no time limit, leaving the layout of each stage as the only obstacle. The player has three lives, and the adventure spans 105 stages; when the game ends, the mole concedes defeat. The design builds on the same company's two earlier mole-digging puzzle games.

t_e8babc1d935c.overview:
Participants guide athletic competitors across a series of cold-weather events centered on high-speed winter action. Five distinct disciplines are featured, consisting of downhill skiing, aerial ski maneuvers, halfpipe snowboarding, inflatable sled racing, and snowball battles. Players can tackle each of these events individually for practice or progress through them sequentially as a complete competition set to earn cumulative scores.

Up to six competitors can participate in the action by taking turns, with play alternating between participants. When a round ends, the next registered player activates either controller to take their turn on the slopes.

t_e8d0e4dbeb4f.overview: An amateur adventurer named Wynn heads alone to Atlantis, a gigantic island that rose from the southern Atlantic Ocean, after learning that his master disappeared there. Armed with the special dynamite his master invented, he must face an evil emperor who seeks to revive an ancient empire and rescue his master in the final zone. The platforming scrolls in both directions and spans 101 zones set in fields, caves, ruins, temples and even clouds. Warp entrances inside each zone lead to others out of numerical order, and secret warps can jump far ahead. Wynn fends off enemies by throwing sticks of dynamite. Every zone has a time limit, and a life is lost on touching an enemy, falling into a pit or getting caught in his own explosion.

t_e9279bcc267f.overview: Two different styles of play are joined in this action game. The first is an overhead segment, comparable to Metal Gear, in which the hero walks through giant enemy bases held by terrorists, firing in the direction he faces and laying down bombs that blow up after a set time. Weapons include a machine gun, a perforation gun and a bazooka with limited ammunition. After finding the exit outside a base, the player pilots the titular Silver Eagle in the second segment, a static-screen shoot-'em-up made up only of boss fights, moving in four directions to dodge each boss's attacks. Bombs and weapon power-ups picked up in the first segment carry over to the second. Four enemy bases make up the campaign, and the final boss is a giant robot.

t_e95824706f51.overview: Roads for a traveling space vehicle have to be completed in this puzzle game. Each phase contains 15 stages, and each stage is divided into four sub-stages whose streets are incomplete. Working against a time limit, the players move the block to finish the streets so the vehicle can travel through them. If the streets are not completed in the required time, or no street is left open for the vehicle, it explodes. Developed by Mega Soft, the game was published in Spain by Gluk Video and is also known in Asia as Magic Block. Up to two players are supported.

t_e964ec42536d.overview:
Rescuing Princess Toadstool from Bowser is the central objective as players traverse the Mushroom Kingdom across eight distinct worlds, each divided into four stages. Controlling Mario, or Luigi in a two-player mode, the player navigates side-scrolling environments, leaping over chasms and evading enemy hazards to reach an end-level flagpole. Environments feature caves, castles, pipes, and underwater stages. Across these levels, hitting marked or hidden blocks from beneath reveals coins or assistive items.

Stomping defeats standard adversaries like Goombas or sends Koopa shells sliding into other foes. The Magic Mushroom doubles the character's size and enables brick smashing, while the Fire Flower grants projectile attacks, and the Starman provides brief invincibility. Gathering one hundred coins or green 1-Up Mushrooms awards extra lives. Every fourth stage concludes inside a castle, challenging players to overcome Bowser, or an impostor in his likeness, over a pit of lava.

t_e97deb2e87e3.overview: Sengoku-era Japan, excluding Okinawa, forms the board for this dice-rolling board game built around Beat Takeshi. Players roll dice to travel to various places around the map, but beyond simple board-game movement there is a contest for territory in which castles are seized, and each game mode sets its own objectives to accomplish. Takeshi himself, called Takeshi-sama in the game, appears throughout to offer advice or get in the way. Events during the campaign trigger mini-games. The standard format is two to four players, with solo play possible against computer-controlled characters.

t_ea1c202663e5.overview: Based on the NHK animated series Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water, this Famicom adaptation is a simulation RPG in which characters and mechanical vehicles from the show serve as units. The player commands this cast in strategy battles, and the clashes between units are resolved through an RPG-style, turn-based system. The campaign spans 50 stages, with an additional hidden stage beyond them. Toho released it in Japan only, and it is a single-player game.

t_ea25ea776e39.overview: Kunio and his schoolmates switch to soccer in this spin-off, built around a tournament among Japanese high schools. The story opens as the long-struggling Nekketsu High soccer team celebrates finally reaching the national tournament. Teams field six players, halves last a minute and a half, and there are essentially no fouls. The player controls one specific field player and gives Pass or Shoot orders to teammates. Each team can use up to five team-specific super shots per half, and these special shots are close to essential for scoring. Fields vary: one rival plays on sand, and another on ice where tackles slide across the surface. A tournament mode with story scenes and a versus mode with the Nekketsu team and four other teams support one or two players, competing or cooperating.

t_ea2d3b5fe410.overview:
An army of alien invaders led by Vile Malmort has planted an Astrotube in New York, and a pair of soldiers takes to the skies to stop them. Played from a side view, the action has the hero flying through the air and shooting at enemies with a gun, while two satellite modules surround the soldier and fire at enemies as well. Stages scroll both horizontally and vertically, and the campaign runs five stages in total, with boss encounters along the way.

A lone player chooses between a male soldier, Silver Man, and a female soldier, Sparks, and up to two players can fight simultaneously. Continues are unlimited.

t_ea653dcd8f37.overview: Namco's arcade obstacle race comes home with a runner who must cross each of 32 rounds before the time limit expires. Running happens automatically, so the player steers, adjusts speed and jumps to avoid Slip Zones that slow him down, Pitfalls that drop him into holes and Crackers that launch him onto his back, while later rounds add Jumbo Tires, moving Walls, Cubes, Mice and bouncing chess pieces. Springboards propel him forward and Skateboards add speed. Kicking drink cans grants bonus points or speed, and jumping on them stops the timer for a few seconds. Every fourth round adds the time left over from the previous three, and running out of time ends the game. After round 32, this version loops back to round 1 with a shorter time limit.

t_eae39a5214b5.overview: A space shooter in which the player's ship battles through a long series of extensive stages. Rapid fire is standard, and collecting any weapon grafts two satellites onto the ship; the satellites fire the chosen weapon and absorb enemy bullets, and they can be attached to the ship's back for homing fire. Weapons include a laser, the strongest but with a narrow radius, a wide beam that covers three sides, and a spread gun that covers a large portion of the screen. The playing field is wider than in most shooters on the system, letting the player pick a lane, though the screen forcefully pulls the ship along when a specific route is required. Levels alternate between wide spaces and tight, almost maze-like corridors, and late in the game the action moves outside over a desert. There is no on-screen display, not even a score.

t_eb4c11ca5a71.overview: Built on falling-block puzzle play in the vein of Tetris, BugTris adds a hunting twist: bugs are hiding inside the blocks, and the main objective is to capture them. Lines containing blinking blocks hold the hidden insects, so clearing those lines releases them, and the player then catches each bug with a net. Once every bug on a level has been captured, play continues to the next level, and the game ends after level 30 is completed. Game Line published the cartridge in Korea; the identity of its developer is unknown.

t_eb57208c5ce5.overview: Waixing modeled its release on the SNES version of Earthworm Jim 2, replacing Jim with a regular kid named Biqi. The stages are Wood Hills, Water Monster Tunnel, Flight, Farm, Mine, Electric City and Puppy Love, adapted from levels of the original. Ammo tops out at 255 bullets, presumably due to memory limits, and movement in Water Monster Tunnel is slower than in the original or other ports. Except for the Puppy Love music, the soundtrack is Waixing's original work, and a scene showing Biqi and the princess appears after each completed level. The single-cart release has a battery for saving progress by pressing Start during play, plus a difficulty option of Easy, Medium or Hard that sets the starting lives at 9, 5 or 2.

t_eb71c9cc7bad.overview: Built from elements of Donkey Kong Country but closer to an original game than a port, Xiang Jiao Chuan (literally Banana Boat) is a Famicom platformer. The player picks either Donkey or Diddy Kong and plays the whole game with that one character, who loses a life after three hits. A jumps, while B attacks, runs, and picks up and throws barrels. A map links eight worlds of two levels each: Forest, Mushroom, Pool, Grass, Cave, Lake, Jungle and Dock, with swimming in Pool and Lake and a mine cart section in Cave. Bosses include Queen B., Very Gnawty and King K. Rool, plus a new mouse that throws spiky enemies. Bananas and 1-up balloons remain from the original, and passwords awarded after each world replace a save feature.

t_eb7e2598adc6.overview: Viewed from a flip-screen overhead perspective, the adventure follows Link through the fantasy land of Hyrule on a mission to rescue Princess Zelda from Ganon. Hidden across the overworld are the entrances to eight large dungeons, each a maze of connected rooms housing a piece of the Triforce of Wisdom and often blocked by enemies or pushable blocks. Link acquires items that increase his abilities, finding many in caves or buying them from merchants; heart containers raise his maximum health and rings reduce the damage he takes. Completing the adventure unlocks a harder Second Quest that changes many locations and secrets and adds new dungeons and tougher enemies.

t_ebb7c34f0357.overview: Planned as a compilation cartridge for the NES, Arcadia VI was meant to hold six separate games. It was never released, and the surviving build is a demo whose cartridge label is dated 24th June, 1991. Four of the six planned games are implemented in it: Tennis, Xerxes, Ghurka and Twin Cam Turbo. The remaining two games of the planned collection are not present in this version, so the build offers only part of the intended lineup.

t_ebc7e2b8b077.overview: Realistic ice hockey is the aim here, with offensive and defensive play modeled as closely as the hardware allows. Referees call major and minor penalties in addition to offside and icing, and even light contact can be punished, while game misconducts may be handed out at random. Each team's attributes for shooting, speed, defense and goalies are shown on the selection screen, and a defensive strategy is chosen before the opening faceoff. Exhibition games can end in a tie. One or two players can take part simultaneously. Outside Japan the same cartridge game was released as Pro Sport Hockey.

t_ec012d089fdb.overview: John, a young apprentice magician studying under Pong, has his training interrupted when strange people attack and kidnap his friend Yuu, and the search ultimately leads to a battle with an evil king who plans to lead a subterranean army. Built as a side-scrolling platformer, the adventure spans five stages, each in two parts and closed by a boss fight. John's default attack is a psychic blast that can be fired quickly as a single shot, charged for a double shot or charged until glowing for a penetrating triple shot. Twelve spells can be selected while paused, each using two or four notches of a magic meter that refills only at stage midpoints or ends. Some spells transform John into an aerodynamic eagleman, a strong lionman or an elusive fishman.

t_ec2b1ba85503.overview: Game Freak's debut title is an action puzzle game built around flipping floor tiles. In this Japanese version the hero, Carton, sets out to rescue his girlfriend Jenny, who has been kidnapped by his younger sister Quinty. At the start of each level enemy dolls appear and wander around, and the characters can flip the floor tile they are standing on or an adjacent one to propel the dolls away; dolls flipped into a wall or an impassable block are destroyed. Every doll must be destroyed to clear a level, and patterns on the floor tiles can be collected or affect play. Each world has ten levels followed by a boss, and the game can be played by one player or by two players cooperatively.

t_ec2ce369d73b.overview: Piloting a fighter through a 3D shooting course, the player destroys enemies and battles the boss Phobos across six stages, each set on a planet of the solar system, starting at Earth and moving outward. Two weapons split the work: the Pulsar handles air targets and the Quasar handles ground targets. Defeating Phobos requires landing five Pulsar shots on its weak point within a time limit; failing restarts the stage, and pausing is disabled while Phobos appears. Two view modes are offered, with Mode A keeping the ship within a fixed frame and Mode B keeping it centered while the background scrolls. There is no story, and after stage 6 play loops back to stage 1 until all lives are lost. One or two players take turns.

t_ece701008b1a.overview: A virtual board game from Sachen and the official sequel to its earlier Millionaire, it supports up to four players. Each player chooses one of eight characters, the number of years runs from 1 to 99, and everyone starts with 50 million yuan. The board is spread across mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea. On a turn a player can use a card, view the board or roll a die, and the landing space decides the outcome: random gains or losses, five-second trivia quizzes, random events, casino mini-games, cards, unclaimed city spaces that can be bought and charge rivals who land there, and investment spaces. A year ends after every player has used 12 turns, when investment profits and losses are settled; once the years run out, awards are handed out and the final winner is declared.

t_ed04d781b22f.overview: Robots built from floating parts face off one on one in this fighting game: every fighter's head, limbs and body hover separately. In the story, Dr. Walnach disappears with the laboratory's seven military robots and announces plans for world domination, so Dr. Eamon remodels the comedy robot Sukapon into a military robot to stop him. Each combatant starts with a full HP meter and two hearts; emptying the meter costs a heart, and a match ends when a fighter has no hearts remaining. Every robot has six basic moves and four special moves that need no diagonal inputs. The single-player Quest mode spans four levels of enemy robots, with harder difficulties unlocked by clearing it, while Versus mode supports one or two players. The roster reaches 36 characters.

t_ed21f21d9cd4.overview: Masashi Tashiro stars as the hero of this side-scrolling action game, setting out with a yo-yo in hand to rescue four princesses: Cinderella, the Little Mermaid, Thumbelina and Snow White. Most of the adventure plays as a typical character-based side-scroller of its era, with jumps that carry an odd sense of inertia, but the final stage switches to a top-down action style in the manner of The Legend of Zelda. The outcome is not fixed: there are multiple endings, one happy ending and four bad endings. The four princesses were modeled on girls chosen through a public audition, and their names appear in the game. Play is for a single player.

t_ed7cd2ec68e6.overview: A young ninja in a red mask, Hanamaru is ordered to solve a string of disappearances of children at a huge leisure park island, and travels there with his robot hawk partner Takamaru. In this single-player side-scrolling action game he jumps and attacks by sending Takamaru at enemies; in sky stages the hawk carries him, and on skateboard stages he damages foes by landing on them. Collected scrolls power four ninja techniques that cost ninja points, and a windmill item grants temporary invincibility and speed. Bosses appear on odd-numbered stages and the last of the 14 stages, and each boss fight is a card battle in which the higher card deals damage equal to the difference. Hidden mole-whacking bonus stages can award a continue.

t_ed829a74040a.overview: Characters from the original Mega Man series compete in a business simulation that resembles Monopoly. Players and the computer AI take turns going around a set of connected circles, buying up property with Zenny and then charging other characters rent when they land on that building. Other characters can buy portions of the same property, which lowers the rent each owner collects, and some spaces hold cards that change the board, such as raising property prices or development levels. The selectable characters include Roll, Dr. Light, Dr. Wily, Dr. Cossack and Kalinka. Depending on the rules chosen, the winner may be the character with the most owned spaces, the most remaining Zenny or the most developments. Both single-player and multiplayer games are supported.

t_edd1c7387b5c.overview: A side-scrolling action role-playing game, Debias casts the player as the modern reincarnation of the legendary hero Debias, chosen by the guardian Aaron and sent to the kingdom of Arumata, which is ruled by a Demon King and three Gorgons. The hero fights monsters with swords, bombs and other weapons, collecting the gold they drop to buy items in shops. Time passes in town, and once night falls the townspeople flee, facilities close and monsters roam the streets. Three realms of water, earth and fire each end with a boss battle, and the final choice decides which of several endings is shown. Progress resumes by password, and continuing after losing all life halves the hero's gold and tech.

t_ede901129f99.overview:
Knocking each colored object ball into a pocket using the cue ball serves as the primary objective across sixty different stages. The game blends traditional pocket billiards with concepts from miniature golf, setting each round on pool tables of varying shapes that occasionally feature obstacles. Players can also adjust the surface friction of the table.

A life is deducted if the player sinks the cue ball or fails to pocket an object ball across three consecutive attempts. Clearing a stage yields an extra life, while sinking a ball on every strike awards two extra lives. Ball values depend on their printed numbers multiplied by a rate modifier that rises with each successful consecutive pot and drops back to one upon a miss. More extra lives are awarded when the rate reaches 20, 25, 30, 35 or more. The run concludes once every life is lost. In two-player games and games against the computer, players alternate turns.

t_ee26352b0db7.overview: Developed by Hwang Shinwei in 1991, Magic Giral brings the adult computer game Emi's Hot Strip Game to the Famicom as a game of Yakyuken, the strip variant of rock-paper-scissors. Each round won against Emi-chan removes one piece of her clothing, and play continues until she is left with nothing on. The cartridge carries the Chinese name 美女拳, while the in-game title reads Yakyuuken. The same game appeared on Golden Game multicarts under the name Wildball.

t_ee3c44224812.overview: Continuing the Minelvaton Saga story, Silva Saga is a turn-based role-playing game in which the player takes the part of the prince Kyral, grandson of the previous game's hero, on a journey to defeat monsters and ultimately the dark god. Allies come in three kinds: companions who travel with the hero, hired mercenaries, and god statues. Alongside the hero's own group, the mercenaries and the statues each form a separate party, so three parties act together, and making good use of the mercenaries and statues is central to defeating enemies. Both the mercenary and statue systems carry over from the earlier game. Progress can be saved, and the game is for one player.

t_ee51a9bfd897.overview: After the castle is attacked, the ninja JaJaMaru sets out to save Sakura and Tono-Sama. His task is to fill a holy Mandala with eight mystical spirits and stop an evil monk from reviving a dark demon. The adventure plays as a top-down action role-playing game much like The Legend of Zelda: instead of random battles, enemies are fought directly in overhead areas with a chain weapon that shoots out like a yo-yo. Progress usually means visiting a town, learning what troubles its people and where to go next, then fighting through to a boss to obtain a new magic. Spells unlock along the way, including an earth spell that lets JaJaMaru dig underground to avoid enemy attacks, and items such as Oil Lamps illuminate dark caverns.

t_ee8b4dee34f4.overview:
A party of assembled adventurers explores the fictional city of Skara Brae to defeat the evil sorcerer Mangar. The antagonist has turned the town into a world of winter and filled its streets, sewers, and dungeons with hostile monsters. Players guide up to six party members through maze-like environments, solving puzzles and locating key quest items.

Turn-based combat yields experience points, which raise character levels, and gold, which buys better armor and weaponry. The roster can include varied character classes like bards, who perform songs that grant group benefits, and spellcasters capable of acquiring advanced magical arts. Progression relies on building character power to survive increasingly dangerous foes and conquer multi-level dungeon mazes.

t_eea87833a605.overview: Running a car company is the subject of a business simulation in which the player, as company president, aims to capture the top share of the market. There are four markets, and meeting each market's conditions unlocks the next. Each year passes through an opening phase, 24 regular turns and an annual settlement. At the start of the year the player can take out loans and design that year's car by spreading 20 points across performance, fuel economy, comfort and styling. Regular turns cover building and selling cars and are followed by random events such as illness, defective products, strikes, currency swings and large business deals. Departments handle hiring workers and salespeople, buying materials, advertising, discounting and factory efficiency, and paid research can reveal rival designs and market needs. The settlement reports results, pays costs and taxes and ranks the companies; running short of cash can mean bankruptcy. The game is for one player.

t_ef3759630c2f.overview:
Ten levels of action span locations such as Times Square, the SoHo Sewer System, and Snowy Central Park, each concluding with an encounter against a lethal boss. Players select either Leonardo, Raphael, Michaelangelo, or Donatello, each outfitted with their signature weapons such as katana blades, sai daggers, nunchakus, or a bo staff. The mission involves fighting through hordes of Foot Soldiers and assorted enemy machines to rescue April and confront Shredder in the Technodrome.

Turtles can walk in eight directions, jump, attack with their weapons, or combine movements to deliver jumping kicks. Wounds deplete a turtle's life meter, though consuming pizzas restores energy. Each turtle begins with three lives, with a bonus life earned for every two hundred opponents knocked out. The game supports single-player action or two-player cooperative play. If a player exhausts their supply of lives during two-player mode, an extra life can be borrowed from their partner. Up to three continues are available.

t_ef57df5b0bfb.overview:
Controlling the protagonist across side-scrolling action environments, the player navigates the setting based on the film Predator. Initial stages leave the player completely unarmed.

Progressing further requires finding and gathering weapons that appear throughout the journey. The player relies on these acquired armaments to advance through the side-scrolling areas.

t_ef9d074dc939.overview: One day a voice calling for help reaches the hero from somewhere, leading into a fortress sealed by the power of a demon king. Rearranged from an arcade action game with role-playing elements added, the quest spans 300 screens of exploration-based action. The goal is to find the demon king, defeat him and rescue a mysterious person; which of three rooms holds the king is decided at random. Only one boy is playable at the start, and other espers rescued inside the fortress join later: a girl who excels at hovering, a strong boy who can break certain walls, a tall boy with the best jump, and a slow elderly man with great attack power. Attacks are made with a hammer. Defeating enemies earns experience, levels rise only after switching to the map screen, and moving between rooms requires touching a statue near the door.

t_ef9e77b66b88.overview: Judo bouts form the heart of this 1990 entry in the Moero!! sports line. The player's judoka must travel around the world in search of judo opponents, and defeating five of them earns a place in the Summer Olympic Games to compete in the judo event. Collecting the gold medal requires beating nine opponents at the Olympic Games, while a record that mixes victories and defeats can instead bring home the silver or bronze medal. Play follows this globe-trotting route from early challengers to the Olympic stage, and both single-player and multiplayer play are supported.

t_efacf659ec44.overview:
Defeating the eight robots that Dr. Cossack has sent to destroy Mega Man is the main goal confronting the player. Controlling Mega Man, the player navigates eight stages selected in any sequence. The character runs, jumps, slides, shoots, and climbs past obstacles and enemies before facing a Robot Master at the conclusion of every stage. Conquering each boss adds that Robot Master's signature weapon to the player's arsenal. Eliminating all eight Robot Masters unlocks two separate sets of linear stages needed to finish the game.

Mega Man utilizes an upgraded arm cannon that charges energy to unleash larger and more damaging blasts. Traversal support comes from the dog Rush, who transforms into three modes, alongside hidden adaptors found within stages. At designated points in certain levels, Dr. Light's robotic suitcase Flip-Top tosses Mega Man a power-up item.

t_efad3f9d0b53.overview: Developed by Open Corp. and released in South Korea by Daou Infosys, this side-scrolling action platformer is set after Earth's explosive population has caused food shortages and pollution. The Earth Federation develops alien planets to resettle humanity, but scientists and troops who reject the new United Nations revolt and seize one of them, so the United Nations dispatches METAL FORCE, a battle robot developed by the Defense Research Institute. Play resembles the Mega Man games, except that the robot never takes enemy weapons. Instead it carries two weapons, a default wave attack and a boomerang, which can be switched and upgraded with power-ups dropped by enemies. The linear adventure spans seven missions on different planets, each ending in a boss battle.

t_f0118e1ff687.overview:
Piloting a spaceship over a looping mountainous landscape, the player shoots hostile alien forces to protect residents situated on the ground. An unlimited laser beam fires straight ahead to destroy encroaching spacecraft, while a limited stock of smart bombs eliminates all adversaries visible on the screen. The main objective centers on defending the residents of the planet Ligaras from abduction by Landers and other aliens, and a wave ends once the aliens are destroyed, though some types may be left alone.

A sparkling square gate also appears on the screen, functioning as a warp portal that transports the spaceship to the other side of the planet, where more enemies await. Players start with three ships and five smart bombs. One or two players can take part, with Game A for beginners and Game B for experts.

t_f039f958fe84.overview: Known outside Japan as Gemfire, Koei's turn-based strategy game is set on the island of Ishmeria. Long ago six wizards sealed a Fire Dragon inside a ruby on a crown called Gemfire; after a tyrant king abused its power, his daughter pried the six wizard gems loose and scattered them, and rival houses now fight to take the throne. After choosing a scenario and a house, the player must conquer the entire map. On the strategy screen each territory gets one action per month, such as hiring or moving troops, developing land, disaster prevention, giving crops to the people, diplomacy or attacking an adjacent territory. Battles are turn-based tactical fights with five units, including archers, knights, horsemen and a wizard or hired unit, won by capturing the enemy base, defeating every enemy unit or exhausting the enemy's food. One or two players can play.

t_f04e57af681f.overview: A sequel to the 1981 arcade game Warp & Warp, this multidirectional shooter has the hero destroy aliens on two different types of levels. In the free-movement Space World, a top-down shooting stage, he fires his gun in four directions and must destroy a set number of aliens to advance. In the obstacle-filled Maze World he cannot shoot and instead drops bombs, whose fuse lasts longer the longer the button is held. Warps between the two worlds open at intervals, though leaving is optional. Unlike its predecessor, power-ups are available alongside new enemy types. Bonus enemies sometimes carry letters, and spelling EXTRA grants an extra life. Two players can play at the same time, one controlling a white Warpman and the other an orange one.

t_f08687f1ad1c.overview: Kunio's crew takes to the ice in this rough-and-tumble hockey game from the Nekketsu series, played three-on-three over three periods of three minutes. Beyond shoulder checks and stick battles, skaters can punch, kick and club opponents with their sticks, and special shots, shock waves and backdrops fly across the rink. Each character also has a charge attack. Players who take repeated hits become enraged, and striking back in that state draws a penalty that sends them off until their team concedes a goal. A scenario mode follows the struggling hockey club of Nekketsu High, which will be shut down if it loses its next inter-school match, as Kunio arranges practice games against other strong clubs. Winning brings new members and power-up costumes. A versus mode is also included, and a second player can control the goalkeeper.

t_f0aeccbfe4ea.overview: Choosing from a list of 25 countries, players take control of a national men's team, pick the team's 11 members from a roster of 15 and select from a choice of team formations. A "Super Cup" tournament mode sits alongside exhibition matches, which can be played alone or by two players, either competitively or cooperatively. No football team or federation endorses the game, so kit colors are not authentic. Compared with the earlier Goal!, the list of nations grows by eight, while that game's shoot-out mode is gone. This French release carries the name and likeness of footballer Eric Cantona on its packaging, with his name prefixed to the title.

t_f0ef4af924e8.overview: Played with straightforward 2D action controls, the baseball here centers on superhuman plays: by spending Ultra Points, teams can throw magic pitches and swing secret hits that no human player could pull off. The lineup includes twelve clubs split between the Century League and the Paradice League, plus a separate Ultra League with squads such as All Central and All Pacific. Versus play allows time-delay attacks impossible in an ordinary baseball game. An edit team option lets players freely set player names, abilities, batting styles and pitching styles within a fixed point budget, building a custom squad to take into games.

t_f1102d514e08.overview:
Five stages of land, sea, and air combat make up the journey toward the enemy fortress. Controlling a combat helicopter to avenge Joe's brother, the player engages opposing aircraft, tanks, foot soldiers, and other targets to earn points. Standard firing and screen-clearing bombs destroy opposition, and helicopters can refuel on a mother ship.

Eliminating specific enemies reveals a weapon system that changes attributes when fired upon, granting items such as missiles, cannon balls, machine guns, or speed and power increases. Players can also rescue hostages, though freed captives award no points. Between rounds, a mission map displays defeated enemies and rescued personnel. Up to two players can participate simultaneously, with a second player able to drop in at any point.

t_f11c56b6327d.overview: Track and field comes to the Family Trainer mat here, with the player's own running and jumping powering an on-screen athlete across four events: the 100-meter dash, 110-meter hurdles, long jump and triple jump. Top speed depends on which row of mat buttons is used, lifting the feet before the start signal counts as a false start, and in the hurdles the runner must jump when white box markers appear along the edge of the screen. A tournament mode pits the player against computer runners in the dash and hurdles, while a second mode lets numerous players compete in all four events consecutively. The mat supports two players at once, and up to six can be registered for each event, taking turns.

t_f1516ab776f3.overview: Milon, a tone-deaf boy from a land whose people communicate through tone, arrives at Castle Garland to find it invaded by the evil wizard Maharito, whose demonic army has seized the castle where Queen Eliza lives and taken the people's musical instruments. Starting on the bottom floor of the four-story castle, Milon works his way upward through its stories, a well, two side towers and the very top, attacking with bubbles that also break soft blocks to open routes, reveal hidden shops and expose items. Soft blocks look identical to solid walls, so progress depends on uncovering secrets. Seven bosses stand in the way, each dropping a crystal that strengthens the bubbles. Lingering outside brings falling lightning, and with only one life and no save points, a single death ends the game.

t_f1681c7b6348.overview: Count Dracula, wearing Reebok Pumps, first has to work his way down his castle while avoiding hostile villagers in this unreleased action game. Villagers can be hypnotized with his vampiric gaze or caught in Rube Goldberg-esque hidden traps sprung by pulling levers; Dracula can then suck their blood and briefly turn into a bat to get through the tower. Reebok Pump power-ups grant a temporary speed boost and the ability to jump over villagers and holes. Outside the castle, a large open town must be searched for his bride, Mina, with maps and compasses from villagers serving as hints. After sucking enough blood he becomes an invulnerable wolf, sleeping villagers can be turned into Vampiresses who lead him nearer to Mina, and keys and flowers open gates and homes. Finding the building that houses Mina leads to the next round.

t_f1910a18e3d7.overview: Monsters roam the country, the people of Edo town are turning into yokai, the Book of Shinobi carrying the knowledge of ninjas has been stolen, and the dragon Ryujin has taken villagers and stopped the rain from falling. The brave ninja JaJaMaru must investigate these incidents, with Princess Sakura eventually joining his side. The hero's first role-playing adventure follows the Dragon Quest model: a top-down overworld, travel from town to town, random enemy encounters and simple turn-based combat that earns EXP and gold. Magic spells are gained in the form of magical jewels. The quest is split into four chapters, with the final one unlocking once the other three are beaten.

t_f19990bb42f4.overview: Naval warfare is the subject of this strategy wargame, in which the player commands a fleet of heavy cruisers, battleships, submarines and aircraft carriers in a recreation of one of the crucial naval battles. The package came with a large map and plastic models of ships and aircraft for keeping track of the engagement. Progress can be saved with the Turbo File, a hardware add-on for the Famicom used to save game progress. No background music is heard during play, and the game is designed for a single player.

t_f1d6b5c4d8f1.overview: Modeled on the Space Sheriff series, this role-playing game stars Blader, a rookie space detective assigned to Earth who must protect the planet from Jadoo, an evil organization bent on invading it. His partner Millie, a fellow space detective, sometimes restores his LE, the game's measure of HP. In place of RPG magic, the Space Police transfer units to Blader after certain level-ups, and spending UE, the equivalent of MP, produces effects such as an instant warp to towns already visited or repairs to his armor. That armor, the Tector, leaves him with no defense once destroyed, and without repair parts battles become very hard. Enemy encounters are very frequent. Jadoo is led by King Jadoo, whose Four Heavenly Kings include Tekkender and Batrad.
